articles.title: The Housing Market Is Nuts
articles.body:
European housing affordability, explained by where the jobs are and where they aren't at NUTS-3 level.
Housing is the single largest expense for most European households. This is not a controversial claim - everyone who pays rent or a mortgage knows it. Food, transport, healthcare: none comes close. The question is not whether housing dominates household budgets, but whether we can measure how much and where.
Eurostat publishes exactly such a measure. The EU-SILC survey asks households across Europe what they spend on housing - rent or mortgage interest, utilities, insurance, maintenance, taxes - and reports the total as a share of disposable income. Here is what it says for the five countries featured in this analysis.
At first glance, this looks like exactly the data we need. It isn't.
This is a country-level average. It flattens the extreme regional differences that define the European housing problem - the gap between Lisbon and Beira Baixa, between Paris and the Massif Central, between Amsterdam and Groningen. And Eurostat does not publish this indicator at any finer level of geography.
Worse, the statistic counts rents and mortgage interest but not mortgage repayment. A household paying €1,500 a month on a mortgage - of which €400 is interest and €1,100 is principal - shows up as spending €400 on housing. The other €1,100, the part that actually hurts, is invisible. And the split between interest and principal depends on the rate, the country, and when the contract was signed - making cross-country comparison unreliable even before we consider that countries have very different shares of owners and renters.
The result is a ranking that should give anyone pause. Portugal - a country going through a severe housing crisis - appears as the least burdened. The Netherlands, where the housing debate is real but less acute, appears as the most. The indicator counts rent in full but only the interest part of a mortgage, so its result depends heavily on how each country's households are split between renters, owners with a mortgage and outright owners - and, among mortgaged owners, on how much of each payment is interest. In Southern Europe, where outright ownership is common, a large share of households contributes no rent or mortgage cost to the average.
Eurostat publishes a second indicator from the same survey: the financial burden of housing cost, where households themselves report whether housing is a heavy burden, some burden, or no burden at all. This indicator is sensational, in the sense that it measures sensations.
When you ask people how they actually feel, the ranking is very different - and the Netherlands moves from one extreme to the other. Only 6% of Dutch households report a heavy burden. In Portugal it is 26%, in Italy and Spain nearly 40%. The calculated statistic and the lived experience point in different directions.
In our analysis we will study regional differences, face mortgage repayments as what they are - a burden - and avoid relying on sensations to draw conclusions. Using metrics built from actual regional data, we will find all these five countries, and their NUTS-3 regions, in positions that better reflect the economic strain linked to dwelling.
Welcome to the European housing data crisis.
"The first casualty when war comes is truth" - a line often attributed to US Senator Hiram Johnson in 1917. Housing crises have their own version: the first casualty is data. You cannot measure a problem for which there is no objective data.
We have already seen how the best available Eurostat indicator - the housing cost burden - produces a ranking that contradicts lived experience. But the problems run deeper. Europe has no comparable, cross-country dataset of housing prices per square metre. It has no harmonised regional wage data at the level where people actually live and work. To build the analysis you are reading, we had to stitch together data from five different national statistical offices - INE in Portugal, INE in Spain, INSEE in France, ISTAT in Italy, CBS in the Netherlands - each with its own methodology, coverage, granularity and reporting lag. Some publish transaction prices; others publish appraisal values. Some report wages at the NUTS-3 level; others only at NUTS-2, requiring workarounds that introduce uncertainty.
Eurostat, the EU's own statistical office, does publish a European House Price Index. It sounds exactly like what you'd need. It is not. The HPI is an index - it measures how much prices changed within each country relative to a base year (2015 = 100). It can tell you that Portuguese prices rose 89% since 2015. It cannot tell you what a square metre costs in Lisbon versus Madrid. You cannot divide an index number by a wage to get affordability. The one EU-wide housing statistic is structurally useless for the one question citizens actually ask: can I afford to live here?
Mapadomo comes to the rescue. "granular housing data for Europe", they promise. The dataset, with data for 2000-2020, is unavailable (as of November 2026).
Then there is the question of knowing where people actually live. Some countries maintain continuous population registers - the Netherlands and Spain update theirs yearly, France has run a rolling annual census since 2004, and Italy has had a permanent census since 2018. But even these registers struggle to track sub-national migration in real time. In Portugal, which still relies on a traditional decennial census, the president and the national statistics office have had a public debate over whether the official population figures reflect reality. A housing policy that cannot track where people actually live is steering blind.
Throughout this analysis, we use regional employment as a proxy for the number of people economically active in a region. Employment data is updated yearly and registered at the workplace, not the residence. It still undercounts - informal workers leave no statistical trace - but it tracks reality better than population figures that lag behind internal migration. In Southern Europe especially, people can hold formal jobs and pay rent in regions where they have no residence permit. The employment register captures at least part of what the population register misses.
Curating comparable price and wage transaction data across member states is exactly the kind of work the European institutions exist to coordinate. They have the mandate, the staff and the budget. Meanwhile, the analysis you are reading - built from raw national sources, cross-referenced and harmonised at the NUTS-3 level for 312 regions - was assembled by a single citizen, working for free, on evenings and weekends. If one person can do it, the absence of an official equivalent might be a political decision. Or is it the inertia of not deciding? Hard to tell.
Transparency is not about data not being secret. It is mostly about data being available at a reasonable effort. The effort to compare regional affordability does not seem reasonable. This text stems from very unreasonable amounts of effort.
To be fair, they did define the NUTS-3 regional classification and they keep employment data updated. While insufficient for illustration of the present housing crisis, both have been useful for this analysis. We cover 312 NUTS-3 regions across five countries; of these, 309 have both price and wage data for the effort calculation, and the combined scatter plots show 306 because four Paris-area départements are merged into a single data point.
Before looking at prices and wages, it helps to see the landscape they operate in. Employment density - the number of jobs per square kilometre - is the simplest measure of economic activity. The maps below show it for all NUTS-3 regions in our dataset. White marks the median density across all regions; blue runs toward the sparsest provinces, red toward the densest.
The pattern is immediate. Jobs cluster in a few places: the Lisbon-Porto coastal strip, the Madrid-Barcelona axis, the Île-de-France blob and its Lyon-Marseille satellites, the Po Valley running from Turin to Venice. The interior is pale. In Portugal, a worker in Grande Lisboa has a thousand employed people per square kilometre around them; in Beira Baixa, ten. That is not a subtle gradient but a rather different economy. The Netherlands is overall more uniform and more job-dense.
This is the map that housing prices have to be read against. A region's affordability only makes sense relative to whether anyone can actually work there.
A square metre in Lisbon costs less than a square metre in Amsterdam. But does that make Lisbon more affordable? Only if the person buying it earns a Dutch salary.
Let's divide the price of the square meter in a region by the wage of that region, using means or medians, depending on what statistic is available. We call this metric housing purchase effort: the number of months of gross salary needed to buy a single square metre. Because it is a ratio of two local quantities measured in the same currency, it allows direct comparison across regions and years, eliminating the problematic effects of regional wage differences and inflation. At the national level, the picture is already telling.
Portugal and France look remarkably similar - around one month of salary per square metre. The Netherlands, despite far higher prices, comes out better because wages more than compensate.
These are national averages. The real story appears when we zoom in to NUTS-3 level - the smallest regional unit for which both housing prices and wages are available. White on the map marks an effort of 0.7 - roughly the threshold at which a 50 m² apartment can be repaid in about ten years at maximum mortgage effort. More on loan repayment in Part eight.
The maps reveal what national averages hide. Within a single country, the variation in effort is often larger than the variation between countries. A worker in the Algarve faces a fundamentally different reality than one in Bragança - same country, same labour law, but wildly different affordability.
What explains the variation? House purchasing effort reflects a demand-supply relationship: when more people compete for limited housing stock, prices rise relative to wages. To lower effort, a region needs more houses per resident. But building more is not always possible - you cannot upgrade buildings from 10 to 20 floors once they are built, and widening a road from four to six lanes does not help if single-lane bottlenecks lie between commuting points. Even when possible, building takes a long time. Population relocation or inflow can happen much faster than supply adjustment, which requires projects, permits, manpower and bricks. Because of this, regions that face continuous increase of demand may never fully adjust - they become dense under constrained supply.
It is worth saying that density brings efficiency up to a point, not indefinitely and not regardless of case-by-case circumstances.
Neither housing supply nor actual demand are reliably measured at the regional level - another data gap. What we do have is employment density: employed persons per square kilometre. In regions that are not overly touristic, this is a reasonable proxy for demand pressure on housing.
When we plot employment density against purchase effort, a pattern arises: denser regions are systematically harder to afford.
Portugal has only 26 NUTS-3 regions. Azores uses a NUTS-2 wage fallback because national wage data is unavailable for this region; plot captions give the number of regions shown, but fallback regions are excluded from the regression fits throughout. A log-linear fit to the 25 non-fallback regions explains 33% of the variation in effort (R² = 0.33). That rises to 82% when we set aside four outliers - Algarve, Madeira, Alentejo Litoral and Alentejo Central - regions where tourism and/or other local factors push effort well above what density alone would predict. Outliers are marked with a red circle in the plot. Colour saturation encodes tourism intensity (overnight stays per worker) - the more saturated the dot, the higher the tourism pressure.
With a sample this small, a handful of regions can move the fit substantially, so the R² should be read with caution. Still, the direction is unambiguous: denser regions come with higher purchasing effort.
Spain provides a larger sample: 47 of its 59 NUTS-3 regions. The missing twelve are the Balearic Islands, the Canary Islands, and the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla, where price or wage data is not available at this level of geography. The four foral provinces (Álava, Bizkaia, Gipuzkoa, Navarra) are included but use NUTS-2 fallback wages, since AEAT does not cover territories with their own tax administrations; these four are excluded from the regression fit, leaving 43. Density alone explains 64% of the variation, that value rising to 76% (R² = 0.757) by excluding touristic outliers Málaga and Girona, and a third outlier called Huesca. The larger sample, with a lower proportion of outliers, allows for a more stable estimate of the relationship.
When we pool Portugal and Spain together - two countries with very different wage levels, price structures and regional geography - the combined sample reaches 73 regions (68 after excluding fallbacks). Density alone explains 50% of the variation (R² = 0.50), rising to 72% when we exclude the five outliers of this combined fit (Algarve, Madeira, Alentejo Litoral, Alentejo Central, Málaga). The relationship survives crossing borders.
Adding France brings 90 of its 96 metropolitan départements. Three are missing because the DVF property transaction database does not cover Alsace-Moselle (Bas-Rhin, Haut-Rhin, Moselle), where a local land registry law predates the national system. The remaining gap is Paris: its NUTS-3 boundary covers only the 103 km² city proper, registering over 21,000 jobs per km² - a density so extreme it compresses every other region to the left of the chart. To make Paris comparable to other capital regions we merge it with the three départements of its Petite Couronne (Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis, Val-de-Marne), weighting by employment. The merged Paris metro unit still leads the density ranking at around 6,500 jobs/km², but the effort index drops from 2.1 to 1.61 - high, but no longer on a mathematical cliff. This is also why we switch to a logarithmic x-axis: even after merging, the density range spans from single digits to thousands. This merge is not cheating: data work is sometimes messy and the NUTS-3 classification is not clean either (see NUTS-3 regions are not equal in the appendix).
With 163 regions across three countries (158 fitted), density explains 64% of the variation in effort (R² = 0.637, excluding 13 outliers). The logarithmic relationship holds across borders, wage systems and housing markets.
And it still holds directionally with all five countries combined, despite the complexity of Italy, the unusual affordability of the Netherlands relative to its job density, and the existing comparability issues (see Comparability caveats in the appendix).
The easy reading of this data is "large cities are expensive." Certainly, prices rise with job density and so do wages. But wages in dense areas don't rise proportionally to housing costs. The gap between what housing costs and what people earn widens as you move toward the economic centres. Then there are the obviously touristic regions: Algarve, Málaga, Girona, Alicante, the Côte d'Azur (Alpes-Maritimes, Var), Corsica, Rimini, Bolzano. These regions are low density, high effort - tourism inflates prices where local wages, driven by a non-touristic job market that is not competitive enough, have no chance of keeping up. These regions are a very specific minority where what happens does not follow the general rule. And they are usually not the ones that include the capital.
Removing these outliers reveals a strong density-effort relationship that holds even when mixing several countries. It does not remove the effect of tourism - it removes the effect of extreme tourism. The regions that remain still feel tourism to varying degrees, and that residual influence partly explains why the fit, while robust, is not perfect: moderate tourism pushes some regions above the density-only trend line without being extreme enough to flag them as outliers. Once we recognise this, the natural next step is not to keep discarding data points but to accept tourism intensity as a second variable alongside employment density.
A multivariate model using only two predictors - employment density and tourism intensity - explains 57% to 85% of the variation in effort, depending on the country.
We can isolate each variable's contribution by fitting for density and tourism separately. The table below shows R² for density-only and tourism-only fits, both with all regions and after excluding outliers.
Density alone explains 34% to 64% of the variation, rising to 61% to 82% after excluding outliers - the touristic regions that break the density pattern. Tourism-only fits tell the opposite story: R² stays below 0.25 for Spain, France and the Netherlands, and the already low values collapse further after outlier exclusion. Portugal's tourism-only R² of 0.57 is driven by the strong pull of a few touristic outliers like Algarve and Madeira - small samples (n=25 fitted) make such anomalous situations more likely; once those outliers are removed, tourism explains essentially nothing (R² = 0.02). Italy is the exception: tourism-only R² is 0.39 with a large enough sample (n=106) to make accidental alignments unlikely, and it holds at 0.27 after outlier exclusion.
Unlike fitting for density, fitting for tourism alone does not expose a small number of outlier regions that could be removed to improve the fit. That's because, apart from Italy where the situation is more complex, tourism-driven regions are the exception, easily identified as outliers when fitting for density.
Comparing the two tables confirms this reading. The multivariate fit (density + tourism) improves on the density-only fit in every country - tourism always adds predictive power. More telling: the multivariate fit also beats the density-only-clean fit (outliers excluded) in four of the five countries. Even after removing the most touristic regions, the result is worse than with tourism as a second variable. The single exception is the Netherlands, which makes sense: it is not a tourism-heavy country, and its outliers are likely driven by other factors.
The takeaway: in most regions, tourism modulates the influence of job density - it nudges effort up or down around a trend that density sets. Only in a handful of regions does tourism override job density entirely and become the dominant force.
Capital regions concentrate a disproportionate share of national employment. Grande Lisboa alone holds 25.5% of all jobs in Portugal. Madrid holds 17.9% of all jobs in Spain, the Paris metro (Paris + Petite Couronne) 15.9% in France. Even in polycentric Italy, Roma accounts for 8.5%, matched only by Milano at 8.2%. Workers do not choose these regions on a whim - they go where the jobs are.
And the jobs are expensive to live near. Capital regions rank among the highest in effort - the Paris metro reaches 1.61, Grande Lisboa 1.30, Madrid 1.27, Groot-Amsterdam 1.09 - driven by the density relationship we have seen: more workers competing for housing in a bounded territory. Tourism-heavy regions like the Algarve (1.86) or the Côte d'Azur (1.42) can rank even higher. To make this concrete, we translate effort into mortgage repayment time for a 50 m² flat.
These are regions where a single earner needs nearly two decades or more to repay a modest flat. Even after combining four départements, the Paris metro requires 37 years. A 75 m² apartment instead? The monthly payment no longer covers the interest. The loan is never repaid. And these timelines cover only the mortgage itself - saving for the 10% deposit and transaction taxes, which add roughly 3% to 12% of the purchase price depending on the country, is time not included in the simulation (see Part eight).
Paris itself is even more extreme. Its NUTS-3 region (FR101) covers only the dense urban core, where the effort index reaches 2.1 - pushing the mortgage calculation to 101 years. But that number sits on a mathematical cliff: at 4% interest, the monthly payment barely covers the interest on the loan. A small rate increase to 4.2% tips it over the edge - the loan becomes infinite. A drop to 3.5% brings it down to 56 years. No other region in our dataset is this sensitive to assumptions, which is why we lead with the Petite Couronne figure instead.
The trap is not just financial. Capital regions are large enough that living on their edge already means a long commute, and living outside them means commuting even further while inheriting some of the inflated housing prices. Workers in surrounding regions earn wages that do not match the centre but face prices driven up by proximity to it. (See NUTS-3 regions are not equal in the appendix for how boundary size affects cross-country comparisons.)
In public debate, tourism is frequently cited as the primary driver of housing unaffordability. Short-term rentals, foreign buyers, holiday apartments consuming the housing stock. The narrative is compelling and, in specific places, not wrong.
The data tells a different story at scale.
Tourism does correlate with higher effort - the multivariate model confirms it has a small, positive coefficient in every country. But as a single variable it explains only 23% of the variation across all five countries (R² = 0.231), and as we saw in the single-variable fit evidence, that number collapses for most countries once outliers are removed.
Despite a similar R² (the five-country density vs effort fit has R² = 0.265), this plot is substantially different from the density vs effort plot for all countries: visually, we don't see a way for improving the fit by removing a handful of data points. Unlike what happens with the density vs effort plot where a clear group is identifiable by eye - even if not automatically marked as outliers - removing the oddities here leads to "vertical data", i.e. no correlation.
There are particular regions where tourism has a strong influence like the Algarve, the Côte d'Azur, the Balearics or Corsica. It is also true that some city centres are disproportionately under pressure, with both employment and tourist demand in the same square kilometres. It is even fair to say that tourism intensity should be actively monitored and managed in all the regions - there are other good reasons, apart from house prices.
Still, the contribution of tourism to the overall picture is secondary. Within each country, employment density - the sheer number of jobs per square kilometre - explains far more of the variation than tourism does. And Europe is not facing a city-centre-only crisis. NUTS-3 regions span entire metropolitan areas, suburbs and commuter belts. When a NUTS-3 region is unaffordable, it means that even workers willing to endure long commutes within it cannot escape the cost pressure. The problem covers the territory where people actually live, not just the postcard downtown. The problem of scapegoating tourism is that we may remain blind to the structural problem of density. And risk overshooting tourism restrictions without achieving meaningful results.
Is there a causal relationship between density and effort? Correlation does not imply causation, but it invites analysis.
When job density and effort move together, three readings are possible: effort causes density, density causes effort, or both are caused by something else.
The first is implausible - high housing costs do not attract employers. The third is more subtle: one or more external factors would need to drive both density and effort in such a way that the specific logarithmic relationship we observe between them is produced across different countries. It is not enough for a confounding variable to merely raise both; it would need to shape them into a specific mathematical form. Explanations based on confounding variables (geographic constraints, cultural traits, ...) would require many things to fall in the right place, with the right intensity, across several countries. The reading that best survives parsimony is the most direct: density causes effort because people need to work and tend to live within commuting distance of the workplace. NUTS-3 regions are typically large enough to contain both workplaces and residences. Within a region, prices react to demand pressure more vigorously than wages do, because building houses takes time and accepting a longer loan feels like a better option than not having a job.
Employment density is the candidate structural driver. Tourism amplifies specific hotspots and influences other regions, but it is not the master variable. Companies open offices where talent lives. People move to where they can work. Demand concentrates. Prices rise. More companies open offices where talent already moved. More people move there. The cycle feeds itself.
For some regions, housing is mathematically out of reach under any reasonable set of mortgage assumptions.
When we simulate a standard mortgage - 90% loan-to-value, 4% interest, 45% of net salary going to repayment - a large share of workers face a repayment period of 15 years or more for a 50 m² flat. This is roughly a studio or small one-bedroom apartment. In Paris and its Petite Couronne, the combined capital region, a 50 m² flat takes 37 years to repay. Paris itself sits on a mathematical cliff where the payment barely covers interest (see Part six). In Lisbon, the simulated average loan repayment for a 50 m² apartment is 24 years.
A 45% effort ratio is unusually permissive. It matches Portugal's regulatory DSTI limit, but exceeds France's 35% limit and the affordability thresholds commonly applied in Spain and Italy. The Dutch system uses income-dependent limits rather than a fixed percentage. The simulation therefore uses a relatively generous assumption, and actual borrowing capacity may be lower.
Furthermore, these figures count only the loan. Before the first payment, a buyer must save the 10% deposit plus transaction taxes and fees - which range from roughly 3% of the purchase price in the Netherlands to 8-12% in Spain and Portugal, with France and Italy in between. Early in a career, when salaries are lowest and savings hardest to accumulate, this can take years. The time required to become a homeowner can therefore extend well beyond the simulated mortgage repayment period.
The simulation pairs one salary with a 50 m² flat. This is a proxy for household effort regardless of household size: a couple earning two salaries would face a proportionally larger home. Household income and composition data are not available at NUTS-3 level, so we hold the ratio fixed - one income, one modest unit - to keep the comparison fair across regions and countries.
In Portugal, three quarters of employment is located in regions where a small flat requires a 15+ years repayment effort. In Spain and France, it is nearly half. Even in Italy, a third. Deposit comes on top. These are the regions where the jobs are. "Move somewhere cheaper" means leaving employment behind.
The metric we use throughout this analysis is original and opinionated. It introduces mortgage simulations based on regional data assembled from national sources and uses a 15-year repayment horizon as the threshold for unaffordability - a cutoff that is, at best, borderline reasonable. We build it because nothing better exists at this level of granularity, but a fair question is whether the picture it paints is accurate.
As a consistency check, we turn to an official source. In the opening section we saw that Eurostat's housing cost burden indicator excludes mortgage principal repayment, making cross-country comparison misleading. The OECD Affordable Housing Database, however, publishes a closely related indicator - the median mortgage burden as a share of disposable income - that includes principal repayment, without mixing in energy, maintenance, or insurance costs. This indicator is not granular - it irons out regional differences, as every national indicator does - and it measures something conceptually different from what we built: rather than estimating potential strain from simulated loans or simple effort ratios, it captures actual burden from self-reported mortgage payments in EU-SILC.
Because actual mortgage payments are sensitive to ECB key interest rates - and a large share of loans in these countries carries variable rates - we use a three-year average (2022-2024) to smooth year-to-year volatility.
The ranking is the same. Portugal carries the heaviest mortgage burden, followed by France, Spain, Italy, and the Netherlands - the order produced by our regional effort metric in Part four. Two indicators built from different data, at different scales, with different methodologies, point in the same direction.
How concentrated is employment today? In Portugal, half of all jobs sit on just 11% of the country's land area. Spain packs them into 13%, France into 14%. And since 2000, the picture got worse for almost every country. In Spain the area needed to cover half of employment shrank by 3.8 percentage points, in the Netherlands by 3.6. Across the EU, the trend is even starker: Bulgaria lost 13 points, Hungary and Finland 12.
Country-level numbers, however, flatten the story. Mapping the change in each region's share of national employment between 2000 and 2023 reveals which regions gained importance and which regions lost.
The pattern is consistent: capital regions and their satellites pull in red, while the interior fades blue. Tracking the top employment region in each EU country over two decades confirms the trend is not slowing down.
We have seen that most countries in Europe increased their employment concentration levels. The maps showed the geography and magnitude of that evolution, region by region. The top-region charts confirmed that capital regions follow this trend. One verification remains: did regions that already held a large share of jobs in year 2000 generally gain more employment share? Let's investigate for the five countries under study.
Every capital region gained employment share - from Paris (+0.5 pp) to Lisbon (+3.7 pp). Among the twelve non-capital regions in this selection, the story is not simple: five gained share (led by Milano at +1.5 pp), five lost (led by Napoli at -0.4 pp), and two were essentially flat (Porto and Brescia). This sample size is, by construction, small, so generalizations are difficult. Increasing the sample by setting the percentage threshold to ~50% would show more regions but does not uncover a clear pattern. In fact, we find that the dynamics of small job share changes on top of small initial job shares to be complicated and highly country dependent. The concentration story is not about all large regions increasing their relative importance - it is about capitals pulling away and runners-up working their ways, with mixed outcomes.
What is the net result? The distribution plots below rank each country's NUTS-3 regions by employment and show how many it takes to reach 50% of the national total. Portugal needs just 4 regions, Spain 7, the Netherlands 8, France 16 and Italy 19.
These plots illustrate well the significant concentration, especially in Portugal, Spain and France. Half of the jobs are in 11% - 14% of the area, for these 3 countries. Italy and The Netherlands show less extreme results, which is compatible with the overall better affordability found for those countries.
The Gini coefficient, a standard measure of inequality that can also be applied to the employment distribution across the regions of a country, confirms the picture: Spain leads at 0.59, followed by Portugal (0.53) and France (0.50), while Italy (0.47) and the Netherlands (0.46) are more evenly spread. A Gini of zero would mean every region has the same number of jobs; a value approaching one would mean all jobs are in a single region.
At this point, we should note that the share statistics are a zero-sum view - we have seen which regions gained relative importance from 2000 to 2023 and we have seen the resulting employment distribution for 2023. But what happened to employment in absolute terms? That last insight will be provided by the following maps.
The employment variation numbers highlight differences between countries. In Spain, nearly every region gained jobs - but the share map shows Madrid ate a significant slice, reinforcing its already dominant share. In Portugal, the interior didn't just fall behind relatively: Douro lost a fifth of its workforce and Trás-os-Montes lost a sixth. Italy and the Netherlands had absolute gains in almost all regions. France shows gains in most regions with losses in a smaller, but significant, number. But there is something in common: every capital region had double-digit growth. Absolute employment gains for capital regions are in the range of 21% (Paris + Petite Couronne) to 48% (Madrid). For the capital regions of these five countries, increased employment share came hand in hand with double-digit growth of employment density, generating outstanding pressure in the housing market.
Two findings stand out.
First, housing purchase effort is structurally correlated with employment density across all five countries under study. The simplest explanation is causal: when more workers compete for the same land, prices rise relative to wages. Second, that pressure has been intensifying. Since 2000, every capital region recorded double-digit employment growth - not as an isolated boom but as part of a broader trend in which the share of national employment concentrated around capitals has increased. More jobs, more people, same land - the mechanism is self-reinforcing.
The chronically lagging supply is not attributable to a single problem. Many have been publicly mentioned: lack of space, permit bottlenecks, manpower scarcity, expensive credit, zoning laws, political obstacles. Whatever mix affects one region is different from the mix of another, even the effect being the same. Some argue for more houses; others argue for price controls. It is hard to imagine that the affordability problem in dense regions will be solved using either simplistic approach. And the more concentration increases the more the solution is dependent on a few regional administrative structures - hostage to whatever logistical issues or political biases affect the dominating regions. As that happens, people will, most likely, remain strained - and productivity, fertility and well-being will suffer. Density and concentration are rarely part of that conversation, which is what motivated this study. Could decentralisation be part of the solution?
The COVID-era experiment with remote work briefly suggested a different future. Workers discovered they could live in affordable regions and earn urban salaries. Housing pressure on dense areas eased, if only slightly. Secondary cities saw new demand. In 2020, the question was suddenly legitimate: do we all need to be on 11% of the land to do our jobs?
That window is closing. Return-to-office mandates, the gravitational pull of face-to-face networks, and policy inertia are reassembling the old pattern. The structural incentives that concentrate employment have not changed: agglomeration economies, headquarters bias, infrastructure investment tilted toward capitals.
Return-to-office mandates, one after another, are not just HR policies. They are housing policies. Every RTO memo that says "three office days in Lisbon / Madrid / Paris" is also a memo that says "and therefore 24/23/37 years of mortgage for a 50 m²". We re-concentrated on purpose, after seeing what de-concentration looked like.
Every fiscal incentive that only rewards a headquarters in the capital, every high-speed line that only connects capitals, every new university campus that opens inside the same 11% - is a peanut in the corner. Employment concentration is the elephant in the house - the structural force that no amount of tinkering with mortgage rates, construction permits, or tourist regulations will fully overcome. The elephant will not move while we keep feeding the corner.
All data is from 2023 except where noted, using the NUTS 2024 classification and boundaries. Eurostat employment and tourism series for 2023 are already published in NUTS 2024 codes for the five countries in this study. French wages use 2022 (latest available). Regions using Eurostat NUTS-2 fallback wages are flagged and excluded from regression fits. Full data and source code are available in the project repository.
All source data is publicly available. Eurostat datasets cover the full EU; national sources cover NUTS-3 regions within each country. The Local copy column links to our downloaded snapshot used for this analysis.
The following datasets are produced by the analysis scripts and underpin the charts in this story. Each file can be downloaded for independent verification.
This analysis requires three datasets at NUTS-3 level for every country: housing prices per m², wages, and employment. No single European source publishes all three. Each country must be assembled from national statistical offices, tax authorities and property registries - each with its own methodology, coverage and access conditions. Portugal, Spain, France, Italy and the Netherlands are the five where the necessary data could be obtained at comparable quality. Germany was investigated but its regional price data (AK OGA) is published only as binned ranges, not as values usable in regression. Denmark's wages are available only at NUTS-2, too coarse for this analysis. Other countries face similar gaps. Expanding coverage is a matter of data access, not methodology.
2023 is the most recent year for which all five countries have both housing prices and wages at NUTS-3 level. France is the binding constraint - INSEE publishes regional wages with a one-year lag, so 2022 wages are the latest available and are used as a proxy for 2023. Portugal's transaction price series (INE 0012235) starts in Q4 2019, making anything before 2020 unavailable at comparable quality. Italy's INPS wage data begins in 2019. Tourism data from Eurostat (tour_occ_nin3) switched to NUTS 2024 codes in 2023, making that the only year where tourism intensity can be matched to the current regional boundaries without manual code reconciliation. The housing cost burden chart uses the same 2023 reference year as the rest of the analysis.
Cross-country comparisons should be read with care. The wage concept differs: Portugal (MTSS Quadros de Pessoal) and Italy (INPS) cover private-sector employees only, while Spain (AEAT) and France (INSEE DADS) include all sectors. The Netherlands (CBS) reports compensation of employees - gross salary plus employer social contributions - which is corrected by dividing by 1.27 to approximate gross salary. Within each country all regions use the same concept, so regional rankings are unaffected.
Housing prices also differ in concept: Portugal and France use median transaction prices from notarial records; Spain and the Netherlands use mean transaction prices; Italy uses expert-appraised market value ranges (OMI quotations), not actual transactions. Mean prices are typically 5-15% higher than medians due to luxury outliers. The Italian figures are methodologically closer to valuations than to recorded sales.
There are also differences between national definitions of dwelling floor area. These include the treatment of common areas in apartment buildings, balconies and terraces, as well as other spaces such as cellars, attics and storage rooms. Consequently, the reported price per square metre is not based on a perfectly harmonised measure of floor area across countries.
Per-country scatter plots and regressions are reliable. The combined multi-country plots are useful for seeing overall patterns but should not be read as precise cross-country rankings.
Visitor nights per worker is a NUTS-3 average. In a capital region, tourists cluster near the city centre while the workforce spreads across the whole metropolitan area, so the metric undercounts tourism pressure where it is most intense and dilutes it across suburbs where it barely exists. In regions like Algarve or Corsica, where tourism is the defining activity across the territory, visitors are more distributed and this average is far more representative of reality. Naturally, when comparing regions, this nuance can only be evaluated qualitatively, because NUTS-3 is the finest granularity we have data for.
NUTS-3 boundaries follow administrative divisions, not a standard grid. Paris (FR101) is 103 km² - just the city proper. Madrid (ES300) is 7,972 km² - the entire province, including sparsely populated countryside. Grande Lisboa sits between at 1,322 km²; Rome covers 5,280 km². This matters most for employment density: Paris registers 21,700 jobs per km² while Madrid shows 484 - a 45-fold difference that is largely a boundary artefact, not a real difference in urban intensity.
Housing effort (price ÷ wage) is more robust, since both numerator and denominator are measured at the same geographic scale and area does not enter the calculation. However, large regions like Madrid average high-effort urban cores with low-effort rural fringes, which understates peak affordability pressure. Paris, by contrast, captures almost exclusively the dense, expensive centre - which is why its effort figure looks extreme even by capital-city standards. The adjacent Petite Couronne départements (Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis, Val-de-Marne) have effort values of 1.1 to 1.3 - still elevated, but far below the 2.1 of Paris itself.
This is why in the cross-country scatter plots we merge Paris with its Petite Couronne into a single employment-weighted data point. The case for merging is straightforward. At 103 km², Paris is the smallest NUTS-3 region in our entire dataset - smaller than any region in Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, or Italy. Even after merging with the three surrounding départements the combined area is just 753 km², still well below the median NUTS-3 area of 4,500 km² across our five countries. The four regions form a contiguous urban mass where housing markets are deeply intertwined: Paris prices would not sustain themselves without the millions of workers who commute from the Petite Couronne every day, and those same workers face housing costs inflated by their proximity to the centre. Treating Paris as an isolated data point overstates its density by an order of magnitude and places its effort on a mathematical cliff where small assumption changes produce wild swings. The merge does not hide the problem - Paris + Petite Couronne still ranks as the highest-priced and densest unit in our dataset - it simply brings the measurement closer to what the other capital regions already capture by default through their wider boundaries.
If anything, this intervention errs on the side of caution: the functional Paris labour market extends well beyond the Petite Couronne into the grande couronne and further, and a case could be made for merging a larger area still. We stop at four départements because they form the obvious contiguous core and because extending further would require judgement calls about where the commuter basin ends - a question that the NUTS classification was supposed to answer for us. None of this is a criticism of the NUTS-3 classification itself. EU regulation requires NUTS regions to follow existing administrative divisions within each member state, and for good reason: administrative units have the data-collection infrastructure, legal authority, and political legitimacy that purpose-built statistical areas would lack. France's départements date to the Revolution, designed so any citizen could reach the capital in a day on horseback - sensible for 18th-century governance, less so for 21st-century labour-market analysis.
Not every country maps NUTS-3 to a traditional administrative division. The Netherlands is the clearest exception: its COROP regions are non-administrative areas designed around commuting patterns. Portugal's Comunidades Intermunicipais are a hybrid - created to coordinate EU structural funding, they have no role in day-to-day governance, which remains with the individual municipalities. But France, Spain and Italy map NUTS-3 directly to long-established administrative divisions - départements, provincias, province - whose boundaries reflect centuries of political history. The Paris merge is our way of working with what we have: not redrawing the map, but acknowledging that one boundary was drawn too tightly for the question we are asking.
Per-country scatter plots and regressions are not affected - regions within the same country are drawn from the same administrative system and are reasonably comparable. The combined cross-country scatter plots use the Paris + Petite Couronne merge described above, which mitigates the most extreme size asymmetry. The x-axis (density) still mixes differently sized containers across countries, but no other region presents a distortion as severe as unmerged Paris.
The effort metric uses gross salary - the broadest wage concept consistently available at NUTS-3 level across all five countries. The exact source differs: Portugal uses mean monthly earnings from employer reports (MTSS Quadros de Pessoal, "ganho" × 14); Spain uses mean annual salary from tax returns (AEAT); France uses gross annual salary in full-time equivalents (INSEE DADS/DSN); the Netherlands uses total compensation of employees divided by headcount (CBS); and Italy uses mean gross pay from social security records (INPS).
These concepts are not perfectly harmonised. The Dutch figure includes employer social contributions, making it broader than the others. The Spanish figure comes from tax returns, which may undercount informal or irregular earnings. The Portuguese "ganho" includes overtime and regular bonuses beyond base pay.
We use gross rather than net salary because net wages are only published at NUTS-3 level in France. For the remaining countries, computing net salary would require modelling each country's tax and social security system - which varies by household composition, deductions, and (in Spain) by autonomous community. Disposable household income is available at NUTS-3 in four of the five countries, but not in Italy, and it includes non-work income (pensions, transfers, investment), which measures something different from what a worker earns. Gross salary, despite its imperfections, is the only metric that isolates worker income at the regional level across all five countries.
Outliers are detected in two steps. First, a log-linear model is fitted to all points (effort against ln(density)). The residuals of this initial fit are then tested using the interquartile range (IQR): points whose residual falls more than 1.5 × IQR below the first quartile or above the third quartile are flagged as outliers. The regression is then refitted without them. This is a standard non-parametric method that does not assume normally distributed residuals, and it is applied independently within each country so that cross-country differences in wage or price concepts do not influence which points are flagged.
Despite the comparability limitations described above, the single-variable fits are strong within each country. When countries are combined, the Portugal + Spain and Portugal + Spain + France subsets offer a good balance between sample size and methodological similarity: the Iberian pair shares a similar housing market structure and data tradition, while adding France extends the sample with a well-documented price source (notarial DVF data) and a comparable wage concept. In both combinations the role of the outliers identified in the individual Portuguese and Spanish fits is confirmed with higher statistical confidence thanks to the larger sample.
The two-variable model uses a logarithmic term for density and a linear term for tourism intensity. The logarithm captures the expectation that density's contribution to housing effort has diminishing returns: workers who pay for housing, whether through mortgages or rents that ultimately reflect purchase prices, are constrained by their wages and by credit rules. After the 2008 financial crisis, banking regulation tightened debt-to-income limits across Europe, not primarily to protect borrowers from high effort, but to protect the banking system from systemic risk. These constraints act as a ceiling: as density grows, effort cannot grow without bound. A logarithm approximates this saturating behaviour.
Tourism intensity, by contrast, enters linearly. The demand that tourism brings to a housing market can be inelastic to price: if a region reaches full accommodation capacity and prices rise, the visitor profile may shift to higher-paying segments rather than the volume declining. The supply of housing is locally rigid, but the pool of potential visitors is drawn from a global market whose purchasing power is large relative to any single region's stock, especially when that purchasing power is time-shared across the same property, as in short-term holiday rentals.
As an empirical check, we fitted the alternative model effort = a · ln(density) + b · ln(tourism) + c, replacing the linear tourism term with a logarithmic one. The R² was lower for four of five countries and for the pooled sample: the linear tourism term provides a better fit, consistent with the argument above.
Part one uses two Eurostat EU-SILC indicators. The first, ilc_mded01, reports total housing costs as a share of disposable household income. Housing costs are defined as rent (for tenants) or mortgage interest (for owners), utilities, structural insurance, mandatory services, maintenance, and housing-related taxes. Mortgage principal repayment is explicitly excluded on the grounds that it constitutes saving rather than expenditure. This means the indicator captures the interest component of a mortgage payment but not the principal component, systematically understating the cash-flow burden for homeowners with active mortgages.
The second indicator, ilc_mded04, is a subjective measure: households report whether housing costs represent a heavy burden, some burden, or no burden. For the five countries in this analysis, the subjective ranking (NL least burdened, ES/IT most burdened) contradicts the calculated one (NL most burdened, PT least). The divergence illustrates how the exclusion of mortgage principal and the averaging of very different tenure structures can produce a calculated indicator that points in the opposite direction of lived experience.

articles.title: US and Rest of World Must Follow China's Lead On Green Energy, Says John Kerry
articles.body:
US and Rest of World Must Follow China's Lead On Green Energy, Says John Kerry (theguardian.com) 97
			
		 	
				Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe -- including the US -- must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year's climate summit. As Cop31 opens -- this year the climate conference is in Turkey -- there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest "five-year plan" adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to "actively participate in and lead global climate governance". Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220 billion, and they should grow again this year; the world's largest emitter is now the world's leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there. Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.  "The only country that has hugely accelerated is China," said Kerry. "The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day."
"[China] realized suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they're moving independently. There's been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump."
For autocratic states without free and fair elections, seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added. "They'll see where the market is going, and they will recognize where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal," Kerry said. "Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels."
He added: "The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they're going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That's the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable."

articles.title: We need more goat sacrifices
articles.body:
Just a quick thing before this week’s post. If you’ve preordered THE STRANGEST IDEA IN THE WORLD, I’d like to send you a little something extra in the mail. Submit your preorder receipt and your mailing address here. This is only available to folks with US or UK addresses—apologies to those who live elsewhere! In the US, everyone with a valid entry will get one; in the UK they’ll pick winners randomly. The link will be open until December 11, and we’ll start mailing things out after that. I won’t spoil the surprise, but I will say that a) it’s very silly, and b) I can’t wait to get mine.
(For the US: US Residents, 18+. Ends December 11, 2026. See terms at https://sites.prh.com/strangestidea-preorder)
Anyway, onto the post!
Before anybody enacts a major social policy or launches any philanthropic programs, they should sacrifice a goat. There ought to be an entire liturgy of grotesqueries, in fact—pricked fingers, names written in blood, robes, candles, chanting, obsidian blades, still-beating hearts, the whole shebang.
The point of this ritual is not to signal our obeisance to the gods (although if any of them want to stop by and help us out, that would be cool), but to remind ourselves that we know nothing. This is procedurally-induced humility, which is desperately necessary, because an alarming number of our best-intentioned interventions do not work.
For example:
- In 2009, Congress spent $3 billion on “School Improvement Grants” for the worst-performing schools in the country. As far as we can tell, those grants did nothing.
- Universities that hired a Chief Diversity Officer between 2001 and 2019 did not end up with more diverse students, faculties, or administrators.
- The American government spent $280 million to help Afghan women get jobs, and now they can’t really say whether any women got any jobs.1
- Remember 20 years ago, when giving laptops to kids in developing countries seemed like the most important thing to do? Well, a 10-year RCT of 531 rural schools in Peru found zero effects of “One Laptop Per Child” on academic performance.2
- Researchers developed four different messages that were supposed to convince parents to vaccinate their kids. None of the messages worked, and one of them accidentally made parents more likely to believe that vaccines cause autism.
Most of those are left-coded failures, so here are some right-coded failures:
- When Arkansas added a work requirement to Medicaid, the number of Arkansans with health insurance went down without any increase in employment.
- In 2002, the Bush administration launched the Building Strong Families Program, which provided counseling to low-income, unmarried parents with the goal of strengthening their relationships, keeping them both in their child’s life, and ultimately getting them married. Three years later, an independent evaluation found that the program did none of those things.
- And here is the effect of four different abstinence-only sex ed programs that run across the United States:
In the social sciences, nothing ever dies; it merely becomes embarrassing. We can’t say that it’s impossible for anything like these programs to ever succeed, given enough time, flimsy theorizing, and generous definitions of “success”. The point is that these effects should be large, and instead they are nonexistent. Seems to me like it’s time to get the goats in here.
HEAVY METAL
It’s inevitable that some of our interventions are going to fail. (If they don’t, we should either be suspicious of the results, or we should be more ambitious with our programs.) What we really want to know is: when we try to improve the world through some policy or program, how often do we succeed?
We don’t have a good answer to this question, but we do have a good joke about it.
In 1987, the sociologist Peter Rossi wrote a tongue-in-cheek paper that accidentally became his intellectual legacy. He would later refer to it as “far from being one of my favorites” and “the source of considerable embarrassment”, and yet it’s the only thing of his that I’ve ever read or even heard of.3 It was called “The Iron Law of Evaluation and Other Metallic Rules“, and it went like this, lightly paraphrased:
- The Iron Law of Evaluation: The net expected impact of a large social program is zero.
- The Stainless Steel Law: Better-designed evaluations are more likely to find null effects.
- The Brass Law: The more a program is intended to change people, the more likely the impact of that program will be zero.
- The Zinc Law: The programs most likely to be evaluated are those most likely to fail.
Rossi tried to walk back his laws shortly before he died in 2006, insisting that there is now a “large number of well conducted impact assessments that yield statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”. Still, even after supposedly enduring 16 years of embarrassment from his one satirical paper, he concluded, “we really do not know whether programs over a wide variety of substantive areas are worth anything”.
Rossi did not do us the favor of actually naming any of those “statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”, and I know why, because I have gone looking for them, and they are not easy to find. The Earned Income Tax Credit, which is designed to benefit low- and middle-income families, was once considered a slam dunk; now a new analysis suggests that it might not do anything. Plain packaging—where you strip cigarette boxes of their attractive branding—seems like a no brainer, but in Australia, it looks like the policy caused smokers to switch to cheaper brands and to smoke more. There’s a reading and math program that has done well in India, but as soon as other researchers tried to implement it elsewhere, the effects shrank.
You can always find a one-off study showing that an intervention works, but if we’ve learned anything from the past 20 years of social science, it’s that one-off studies ain’t worth much. It’s so easy to juice your stats and journals are so hungry for positive results that entire literatures can be suspect, and decades of research can culminate in a shrug. “Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t, it depends on all sorts of factors that we can’t really specify, so uh, good luck!”
Even if we take Rossi at his word and there are as-yet-unnamed programs out there that are reliable and effective, the question still remains: why aren’t there more of them? Why do so many of our best-laid plans end up like this:
OJ A-OK
The answer lies, I think, in a 50-year-old study that is almost certainly false.
One of my favorite genres of psychology experiment is called something like: “the study is probably bullshit but the effect is probably real”. At the top of that heap is The Illusion of Control, a classic from 1975 and a favorite of Psych 101 classes everywhere. Usually, this study gets summarized as “people value their lottery tickets more when you let them pick the numbers vs. when you pick the numbers for them.” It’s as if people think that the mere act of picking imbues their ticket with a bit of juju, which makes them less willing to part with it.
That would be a beautiful study, but it wasn’t the study that was actually conducted. The “lottery tickets” in question were in fact football cards, each one with a picture of a player, their team, etc. Some participants were given the opportunity to choose their football card and some had a card handed to them. Later, just before the drawing, all of the participants were asked how much it would take to buy their card back. On average, the pickers asked for $8.67, while the not-pickers said $1.86.4
I’m sure you can see the obvious and less exciting explanation for these results: when people were given the chance, they picked their favorite players. The people who didn’t get to pick ended up with a card they liked less. This “illusion of control” effect is merely a “reality of people having preferences and acting on them” effect.5
Unsurprisingly, well-powered, preregistered replications with actual lotteries have failed to find any difference in picking vs. not-picking. So that’s that: there’s no such thing as the illusion of control.
Except...obviously there’s an illusion of control! Look around! People will blow on their dice at the craps table, they’ll don their lucky undies when the Knicks go to the finals, they’ll scream “look out!” to the hapless protagonists of a horror movie. When I was a kid, my parents used to send me off to play arcade games without any quarters, knowing that I would simply move the joystick in synchrony with the demo playing on the screen, convincing myself that I was causing the characters to move, when in fact I was merely mirroring them.
Put it this way: why do you think The Secret has sold over 30 million copies? It ain’t the beautiful prose or the sterling scientific evidence. It’s because when Rhonda Byrne tells you that “your thoughts are the primary cause of everything,” it feels kind of true. After all, can’t you jinx yourself by thinking the wrong thing? Haven’t you ever been like “whatever you do, don’t spill this soup” and then the next thing you know you’ve got a shirtful of bisque? And if brainwaves are powerful enough to spill soup, who knows what else they might do!
So no, people don’t believe they can magically improve their chances of winning the lottery by picking the numbers themselves. Still, our intentions feel more potent than they should, and this shows up not only in our harmless superstitions, but also in the way we keep meddling in each other’s lives despite having no idea what we’re doing.6
How do I know my preferred policies will have their intended results? Well, because I intend them. That’s not really my answer to the question; it’s the reason I don’t even think of the question in the first place.
GEORGE W. BUSH, PROPHET OF OUR TIME
Here’s the real evidence of our illusion of control: we’re so certain our interventions will work that we forget to check whether they do at all.
For instance, the National Science Foundation funds over 1,000 STEM education projects, which are aimed at improving curricula, training, student outcomes, etc. According to an analysis by Stuart Buck, 76% of the time, the researchers running those programs don’t even attempt to evaluate them with actual experiments. Apparently if you have a bright idea about how to teach kindergarteners to code, you don’t need to bother assessing it. It turns out George W. Bush was actually right when he said:
Speaking of the government, according to a report from the Government Accountability Office, many federal programs don’t even define their goals, let alone collect data on their progress toward those goals. For instance, the Department of Homeland Security is supposed to stop people from producing and distributing illicit fentanyl, and so they do things like search people’s cars and walk around with drug-sniffing dogs. When DHS was asked, “How do we know any of this is working? What would success even look like?”, they were like “hmm great questions”. They hadn’t set any goals or collected any data, despite being required to do so by law. As the GAO puts it with characteristic mildness: “As a result, DHS’s ability to fully understand the effectiveness of these efforts is limited.”
Maybe it’s too much to expect that the Department of Homeland Security, especially in its current incarnation, would try to figure out whether it’s doing things that actually work. But it’s certainly not too much to expect of private philanthropists, who choose to give away their money of their own free will. Certainly they would care whether their dollars do anything. Right?
Wrong. In 2018, Kenneth Langone, the Home Depot billionaire, donated $100 million to eliminate tuition fees at New York University’s main medical school. This was supposed to encourage med students to pick lower-paying specialties like pediatrics and primary care, and it was supposed to attract lower-income students to medical school in the first place. But neither of those things happened. The makeup of the student body hasn’t changed, and they’re picking the same specialities they always did.
In this case, it should have been easy to foresee that those beaucoup bucks were going to do bupkis. First, medical school is already a good investment, regardless of income: yes, you take on a big pile of debt, but you also make a much bigger pile of money, even in the lowest-compensated specialties. Second, wiping out that debt does almost nothing to reduce the disparities between specialties: the average orthopedic surgeon earns $564,000 per year, while the average family practitioner earns about $281,000. If both of them work for 30 years, the surgeon earns about $17 million, while the family doc earns about $8 million. Meanwhile, the average medical school debt is about $200k, which is nothing compared to an extra $9 million over the course of your lifetime.
And remember: in this situation, both the surgeon and the family doc attend for free, regardless of how much money they had when they arrived, or how much money they make after they leave. So there’s no reason why free tuition should encourage anybody to do anything differently—except to apply to NYU in the first place. And indeed, applications are up 47%.7
To be clear, giving away dunderheaded donations is better than a lot of things that billionaires could be doing with their money, like buying a second superyacht or digging an additional doomsday bunker so they have a place to summer after the apocalypse. I’m glad that the plutocrats are trying to do something nice. I would just like them to succeed.
THE GREAT BARRIER, GRIEF
When people see our big heap of failed interventions, they tend to go through three stages of grief.
- Bargaining
Okay, fine, these high-minded, utopian interventions don’t work, so what we really need is Common Sense and Obviously Good Ideas. For example, if you want to make poor people better off, you should give them money. That’s just Common Sense! That’s an Obviously Good Idea!
Unfortunately, large, well-designed randomized controlled trials keep finding null effects of unconditional cash transfers. In one study, when low-income participants got $2000 with no strings attached, it made them less happy compared to people who got $500 or nothing at all. Psychologically, receiving 20 Benjamins was about 25% as bad as losing your job during the pandemic. That finding might be a fluke, but it also showed up in a study where researchers wiped out a bunch of people’s medical debt and it maybe made them more depressed.
These programs do succeed in sense that when you give people more money, they have more money, and they spend it on things that they need. It’s just surprisingly difficult to find any evidence that having more money makes a difference. (Though note that results are more promising in low- and middle- income countries.)
- Denial
This is where people typically raise the no true Scotsman defense: if we get bad results from a good idea, it must be because someone screwed something up, not because the good ideas were actually bad ideas. Maybe the measures were wrong, the implementation was shoddy, or the people who benefitted didn’t fill out the followup survey for some reason.
This response isn’t totally irrational; programs go pear-shaped all the time. Maybe your One Laptop Per Child program only failed because all the laptops got stolen out of the back of the truck. Case in point: in that medical debt study, it seems like 76% of people didn’t even realize their medical debt had been wiped out. (But don’t get too excited: if anything, calling people and informing them of this boon made them slightly more depressed.)
The real problem with no-true-Scotsman-ing these studies is that you must subscribe to the dubious belief that some tiny tweaks will somehow unlock giant effects. This is a holdover from pre-replication-crisis psychology, back when we thought you could, say, subliminally flash an American flag at someone and make them more likely to vote for a Republican two weeks later. It now seems like rinky-dink interventions tend to have rinky-dink effects, or none at all. So yes, we could always pick more appropriate measures, and the facilitators delivering the intervention could always have a bit more pep in their step. That might be enough to make a program slightly more effective, but it’s not enough to turn a null result into a blockbuster.
- Acceptance
Acceptance sounds good, but it isn’t. Once we realize how hard it is to improve people’s lives, it’s tempting to believe that doing so is simply impossible, and so we are excused from even trying.
This is a bit like finding out that bloodletting doesn’t work and then concluding that no medicine can ever work. (“Well, We’ve Tried Everything”, Says Society That Has Only Tried One or Two Things.) The social sciences are still in their alchemical stage. We do not understand the fundamental workings of the human mind, let alone what happens when those minds combine in societies and economies. Imagine trying to cure cancer using Galenic medicine or trying to land on the moon using Aristotelian physics—that’s what we’re doing when we roll out programs designed to change human behavior.
FULL THROTTLE ARISTOTLE
That doesn’t mean our ill-informed attempts can never succeed. Both Galen and Aristotle were right about some important things: it was Galen who figured out that urine is produced by the kidneys, rather than the bladder (as was commonly assumed), and it was Aristotle who successfully described how objects move in fluids, even if he attributed it to the wrong forces.
But if we want to solve real, Hydra-headed problems, we need more than a handful of facts. (“Doc, I’m all itchy and covered in spots! What do I do?” “Hmm...did you know that urine is produced in the kidneys?”) Until psychology and its neighboring disciplines grow into scientific maturity, all we can do is guess and check. There’s nothing shameful in that, but there is something shameful in pretending otherwise.
This is hard for us to internalize, because by default we assume that we were born near the end of history. We understand, of course, that we still have a few things to figure out, but emphasis on the few. Just look at our beautiful universities, our begowned scholars, our numerous and inscrutable papers! How can you say we know nothing when we have so many TED talks?
We misunderstand what it feels like to be in the middle of things. Almost no one who read Galen or Aristotle ever thought to themselves, “oh, obviously this is only version 0.1 of our knowledge, all of this is tentative and incomplete, and one day it will be overturned and replaced with something better, something that actually works.” No, they thought to themselves, “Thank u Mr. Aristotle for your many true and useful facts.”
That’s why the worst possible reaction to a failed intervention is resignation. We may not know enough to improve our lot right now, but perhaps we could figure it out, if we tried. Maybe that means another RCT, or maybe it means another century of futzing around in the fundamentals before we can do anything useful.
(This does put a ceiling on the utopia we can expect to achieve in the near future. If you believe that we can perfect human nature by reorganizing society to your specifications, you would do well to remember that, as of now, we can’t even get people to go to the gym.)
That may seem unfair—what a bummer to be born in medias res, when so many of our problems remain unsolved! But if it is an affront, every human before us has been similarly affronted, and some of them chose to begin the work anyway. Whenever we pluck a low-hanging fruit today, it’s only because someone else planted a seed that they never got to harvest. So why should we expect to pluck without planting?
As Seneca put it nearly 2,000 years ago:
I revere the discoveries of wisdom and their discoverers [...] For me those things were acquired, for me they were labored for. [...] Let us make larger what we have received. Let this heritage pass from me to posterity increased.
I know some people don’t feel this way. Some believe that the answers are simple and known and merely need to be enacted by force. Others think the answers are unknowable and will remain so forever. For those folks, I offer an invitation: the next time we conduct the ritual before undertaking some new policy, they may have the honor of playing the part of the goat.
Of course, that sum is negligible compared to $4-6 trillion we spent trying and failing to turn Afghanistan and Iraq into thriving democracies.
How times have changed: I know parents who spend hours commuting every day just so their kids can attend a school that won’t issue them a laptop.
Other times an academic made a joke that went on to become their most prominent work:
- In 2009, four neuroscientists published a poster—not even a paper!—showing that, with fMRI techniques that were standard at the time, it was possible to detect activity in the brain of a dead salmon. As far as I can tell, this is one of the most-cited publications, if not the most-cited publication, for every single author.
- Andre Geim won the Nobel Prize in 2010 for his work on graphene, but when people stop him at conferences they want to talk about that time he used diamagnetism to make a frog float.
- Stigler’s Law of Eponymy: “No scientific discovery is named after its original discoverer.” Named after Stephen Stigler (and by Stephen Stigler), originally discovered by Robert Merton. Cited more than most of Stiglers other papers.
- Goodhart’s Law was originally a “jocular aside“ in a paper about monetary policy, and is now the claim for which he is best known.
$68.09 and $15.39 today, respectively.
There are five other studies in the paper that purport to show similar effects, but none of them inspire much confidence. Most of these studies have like 15 participants in each condition, which is not enough to detect big honking effects like “people have more lapses in attention when you deprive them of sleep for 24 hours” (required N = ~28 well-rested people, 28 sleep-deprived people).
In this way, I think the illusion of control may be another triple-decker fallacy, much like the one I described in Bamboozle Me, Daddy:
- There’s the illusion of control: people assume they have more influence over the course of events than they really do
- An illusion of the illusion of control: The original demonstrations of the illusion of control were probably flukes or fraud
- And an illusion of the illusion of the illusion of control: Nevertheless, people still seem to believe they have more influence of the course of events than they really do, and so if you believe there is no such thing as the illusion of control, you are probably subject to an illusion yourself
And after this resounding non-success, Langone donated another $200 million to also eliminate tuition at NYU’s separate Long Island School of Medicine.

articles.title: Greg Kurtzer's Ginux is now a userspace kernel
articles.body:
Ginux is a configurable userspace kernel for isolated Linux compatibility instances. It runs as an ordinary Linux process and places an explicit, versioned contract between managed workloads and the host kernel.
Important
Ginux began as an independent Rust kernel that booted directly through UEFI
and ran a Rocky Linux 10 userspace. That research phase is complete. Its
final source is permanently preserved on the
bootable-kernel
branch and at the
bootable-kernel-final
tag. Active development now continues here as a userspace kernel.
The standalone-kernel experiment proved that an AI coding agent, directed by an experienced human through architecture, gates, and executable tests, could construct a new kernel capable of running meaningful Linux userspace. It also made the limits of that result obvious.
Linux is much more than source code. It is a stable interface, a development process, a global community, vendor and hardware alignment, and decades of compatibility and operational experience. Reimplementing kernel mechanisms does not reproduce that ecosystem, and competing with Linux was never the goal.
The more useful result is the boundary the experiment exposed. Linux must preserve a broad userspace ABI; as Linus Torvalds put it, “And we simply do not break user space.” The kernel regression documentation records that rule. Ginux can sit above Linux and deliberately offer a smaller contract to each managed instance. Before a managed syscall has a host effect, Ginux decides whether to emulate it, perform a validated mediated operation, or deny it.
Put bluntly: Linux must not break userspace; Ginux is designed to break the full Linux ABI guarantee deliberately and selectively. A instance receives only the capabilities and interface behavior its approved workload requires. Human-Directed Agentic Engineering (HDAE):
human-owned product intent, architecture, constraints, and acceptance
boundaries combined with agent-executed implementation, diagnosis, and test
loops. Each approved gate records its scope, non-goals, acceptance criteria,
verification, evidence, and stopping point in hdae/.

GPT, and Greg. To keep the author's ego within its configured resource limit,
the G officially stands for GPT.

NOTICE.

change privileges, and a kernel with close_range (Linux 5.9 or later).

assignments are not implemented by this command and are rejected.

group stops fail explicitly. Audit output is capped at 64 KiB plus a truncation
notice. This path does not implement resource quotas from the instance metadata.
