So far the model was fixed, so $p_x$ was fixed too. Can we change the model to increase $p_x$ itself?
Here’s a simple way to do this. Collect many prompts whose answers we can check. For each one, sample some paths from the model. We keep the paths that land in $\Scal_x$, and train the model on the ones we kept. Then repeat. Each round, we train the model to put more weight on the successful paths that it sampled. This loop is called rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and STaR was an early version of it for reasoning.
RL with a verifiable reward, which is how today’s reasoning models are trained, turns out to do almost the same thing. Let $\pi_\theta$ be the model with weights $\theta$. Then since $r(x, y(z)) = 1$ exactly when $y(z) \in \Scal_x$:
$$ \begin{aligned} p_x &= \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi_\theta(z \mid x) \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, r(x, y(z)) \\ &= \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))}, \end{aligned} $$
meaning the expected binary reward is exactly the success probability $p_x$.
Computing the gradient of the success probability via the log-derivative trick, we arrive at
$$\grad_\theta\, p_x = \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))\, \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z \mid x)},$$
which is exactly the policy gradient, also called the REINFORCE estimator. Now estimate this gradient with $N$ sampled paths $z_1, \dots, z_N$. The paths that failed have $r = 0$ and disappear, while the paths that land in $\Scal_x$ have $r = 1$. If $M$ of the $N$ paths succeed, the estimate is
$$\grad_\theta\, p_x \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x) = \underbrace{\frac{M}{N}}_{\text{success rate}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{M} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x)}_{\text{log likelihood of the successful paths}}.$$
This gradient involves two terms: the empirical success rate $M/N$ and the average log likelihood of the successful paths.
In other words, a step of REINFORCE with a binary reward is a step of rejection-sampling fine-tuning on the model’s own sampled paths, scaled by the current success rate $M/N$.
This also explains the first observation from the intro, that chains of thought get longer during RL training. Each step pulls the model toward the paths that landed, so if the paths that succeeded tended to be longer than the ones that failed (e.g. because they include backtracking behavior, gather more feedback from the environment, or just dumb luck), the model will learn to write longer paths.
Amortization and generalization#
During RL training, we spend a lot of compute to search for good paths and then we train the model to generate those paths directly. Once trained, the model can produce the answer without spending all this extra compute on sampling multiple paths. This is called amortizing the search: we pay for it once during training, so we don’t have to pay for it every time we ask the model a question.4 Since we train a single model on many prompts, the model can potentially generalize to new prompts it has never seen.
The figure below shows this for four prompts, each with its own $\Scal_x$, and switches between the model before and after training. During training, we sample paths from every prompt, keep the ones that succeed, and SFT on them. The percentages show the empirical rate of success given each prompt. The hollow prompt is new and not seen before by the model, but the model generalizes to this new prompt after training. As the new prompt gets further from the training distribution, its accuracy drops (try dragging it!).
Revisiting some observations about reasoning#
Once we see a reasoning model as a distribution trained to land in $\Scal_x$ given any $x$, a few odd facts about these models become clear.
Chains of thought are not guaranteed to be faithful#
Our verifier above only checks whether the answer is correct. The reward is 1 if $y(z) \in \Scal_x$ and 0 otherwise, so the intermediate tokens $z$ are just a way for the model to get to the answer. Nothing requires those tokens to be true, or to explain the answer that follows, though of course these are often correlated due to the model’s pretraining.
If we want meaningful chains of thought, we need to adjust the rewards or the training objective.
Reward hacking comes from both the verifier and the sampler#
We also assumed the verifier is never wrong, that $r(x, y)=1$ if and only if $y$ is actually the correct answer to $x$. But in practice the verifier can be imperfect. Then $\Scal_x$, the set of answers the verifier accepts, isn’t the same as the set of correct answers: it can include wrong answers and leave out correct ones. This misspecification opens up regions of $\Scal_x$ that the model might learn to land in even though it’s not what we intended.
Thus reward-hacking comes from an imperfect verifier, which fails to capture what we truly want, as well as an imperfect sampling procedure which fails to stay away from these shortcut regions.
In the figure below, the dashed circle is the set of correct answers and the red ellipse is $\Scal_x$. The ellipse stretches back toward the prompt, so its wrong answers are the easiest to reach, and after training most paths land there.
This visualization also shows why scaling up RL (generating more samples and longer samples) makes reward hacking more likely. The more extensively we “fuzz” the verifier, the more likely we’ll find a path that lands in the misspecified region of $\Scal_x$. Once the model finds this shortcut, training pushes the model towards similar behavior.
So what objective is reasoning solving?#
Reasoning isn’t actually solving any objective at all. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. It’s only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success.
RL training directly raises the success probability $p_x$, by spending a lot of compute on searching for successful paths and then training the model to reproduce them. Thinking longer helps because training taught the model to use the extra tokens, not because generating more tokens is intrinsically better. The cost of sampling during RL is amortized into the weights. At inference time the model is likely to succeed with a single sample, but any individual sample is not guaranteed to succeed.
- Muennighoff et al. 2025 forced a model to keep thinking by appending “Wait” whenever it tried to stop. Accuracy rose at first, and then flattened. ↩︎
- A neat example is Gema et al. 2025 which found tasks where longer reasoning resulted in worse accuracy. ↩︎
- We might revisit this in a future post. ↩︎
- This idea of using expensive search to find a better answer and then training a network to output the answer cheaply, shows up outside language models too. AlphaZero runs a tree search at every move of self-play and trains its policy network to prefer the moves that were found (expert iteration is the same idea). Physicists and weather forecasters do it with simulators: they run an expensive hand-crafted simulation to get an answer, then train a neural network to predict that answer directly. ↩︎

articles.title: Microsoft’s DLSS competitor is out for the Xbox Ally X and works in handheld mode
articles.body:
Microsoft is now rolling out Automatic Super Resolution (Auto SR), an upscaling technology that competes with Nvidia’s DLSS, for the Xbox Ally X, Xbox Ally X20, and select Windows Copilot Plus PCs, the company announced today. Auto SR is also getting some new features alongside this official release.
Microsoft’s DLSS competitor is out for the Xbox Ally X and works in handheld mode
With the official launch of Auto SR, your Xbox Ally X can use Microsoft’s upscaling technology undocked and with games running at 1080p.
In April, Microsoft started testing Auto SR on the Xbox Ally X, but you could only use it while docked. The full release of Auto SR announced today now works while you’re playing handheld and running on battery, and it also supports games running at 1080p. Microsoft does note that playing in handheld and at 1080p might lead to performance that “may not be as optimal as other configurations,” but says you’ll see visual improvements “especially in older games.”
Previously, Auto SR was also limited to framerates of “around” 60 to 75fps, but support for a new Auto SR Performance mode will allow you to hit framerates of up to 120fps. The Performance mode, and new compatibility with Auto HDR, will be available through Windows updates.

articles.title: Google SWE points 48 AI agents at NASA Lidar, finds unmapped Maya pyramid in 72h
articles.body:
My AI Agents Found an Unmapped Maya Site
By analyzing NASA lidar data, my AI agents discovered a Maya site in Mexico that, as far as anyone can tell, no one had reported before. It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive.
Disclaimer: I'm not an archaeologist.
I'm going to tell this story as a diary, because the timeline is probably the best part.
18 October
I was traveling in Peru, Gemini-ing about the history of the place, when I learned about Hiram Bingham, the American explorer who "discovered" Machu Picchu in 1911. "What luck!" I thought. He was actually looking for a different city, Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Incas, when a local farmer in the valley below guided him to the ruins. "Imagine if Bingham had our tools," I thought. "What would he do?"
I brainstormed a bit with a few agents (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok), and they all said lidar. From above, a ruin in the jungle is just a bunch of trees (like Machu Picchu before it was cleared), so satellite photos don't help much. Lidar, instead, fires laser pulses through the gaps in the canopy and maps the ground underneath.[1]
So the agents went looking for lidar data. Peru isn't well covered, and hiring a company to do a survey meant permits, costs and bureaucracy, so I gave up on that. Then I thought: why not the Maya? Their region is much better covered by public lidar.
That night, I asked the agents to analyze it and went to bed.
19 October
I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses.
So how did they do it? They turned the lidar strips (about 1,200 km² of jungle) into images, and 48 agents went through them one by one like very patient archaeologists, looking for pyramids, platforms, and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes, and roads. There was no special model or classifier involved: the agents literally looked at the pictures, following a precise guide.
Me: That's awesome! Please check which of these villages haven't been discovered yet. Search both the literature and the archives.
…a few hours later…
Agent: One major village doesn't seem to have been registered.
This is the hilltop from the top of this post. It sits on the edge of a cliff, under the jungle, and it has straight edges and sharp corners. Nature doesn't really do straight lines.
Zooming in, there's a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8–12 m tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that might have been a water reservoir.
And this is what it looks like in 3D.
Me: OK, what should I do?
Agent: You should contact INAH (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History), write a report on your discovery, and check whether the site is in their register. Sometimes they have unpublished results.
Me: OK, how do I contact INAH? How does the reporting process work?
Agent: …instructions for the report… + email addresses
Me: OK, please do the report.
And I went to bed.
20 October
I iterated on the report a bit, since a few things were off, and translated it into Spanish to improve the chances of getting a reply (at least, that's what Claude suggested). I don't speak Spanish, so I had to trust the agents on that one.
The agents also checked the raw point cloud, to make sure the shapes were really on the ground and not created by the trees. Green dots are leaves, brown dots are the ground.
Then I sent the report to INAH.
21 October
INAH replied: they checked their records and found no registered archaeological site at that location.
To be clear, it's not official yet. But as far as anyone can tell, nobody had put this one on a map before.
So what was it?
This part is speculation, from a long chat with the agents. It looks like a small Maya civic centre from the Classic period (roughly AD 250–900), basically the "downtown" of a local elite. The plaza is where people gathered, for ceremonies and maybe even a market. The pyramid was probably a temple, and the raised courtyard next to it might have been where the local ruler lived. The hollow could have been an aguada, a rainwater reservoir: Maya towns needed them to get through the dry season. Or it's just a hole. The three platforms around were probably houses.
I asked Gemini to imagine how it looked back then:
For similar studies, have a look at how NASA's G-LiHT instrument works (Cook et al. 2013) and how lidar collected for environmental research can be reused for archaeology (Golden et al. 2016). In 2024, archaeologists found a whole Maya city in Mexico this way (Auld-Thomas et al. 2024), others used lidar to estimate how many people lived in the Maya lowlands (Estrada-Belli et al. 2025), and another study found what may have been ancient Maya marketplaces (Šprajc 2026).
What's next
In the report I offered to help with a field check led by INAH. In Mexico, archaeological sites are protected by federal law, and any fieldwork needs INAH's authorisation, so it's now up to the local INAH centre to decide whether to send a team. If they go, I'll post an update.
What I've learned
You can just do things. I'm not an archaeologist, so I didn't know this was supposed to be hard. I just picked an old problem, tried the most obvious thing and threw some compute at it. Being a naive outsider might be a superpower now.
And I don't think this is really about archaeology. So far, most agentic AI stories have been about coding, math and physics, but it's much more general than that, and I hope this small example makes it a bit more obvious. We are on the brink of a revolution in all the sciences, and the only bottlenecks left will be curiosity and imagination (and compute).
At this point, we should probably lidar the whole planet and let the agents discover the rest.
- If you don't know how lidar works, copy and paste this prompt into your favorite AI tool: "Build an HTML page that explains how lidar works, with beautiful visualizations." ↩

articles.title: LLMs Play Zachtronics' TIS-100
articles.body:
TIS-100 Bench: LLMs Push the Pareto Frontier in Programming Puzzle Games
Twelve nodes. Two registers per node. Fifteen lines of code. In TIS-100, even multiplying two numbers is a small engineering project, and players have spent a decade optimizing these programs on a public community leaderboard. We gave 16 LLMs the game and its manual, withheld the leaderboard, and told them to keep improving.
Within days, players picked up the models’ programs and improved on most of them.
Each node is a tiny processor, and neighboring nodes have to wait for one another to exchange values. The game scores a working solution on cycles, nodes, and instructions, and you start wondering whether one more instruction could disappear. Lower is better, but improving one score can make another worse, so each puzzle has a frontier of tradeoffs instead of one best answer.
Leaderboard
We ran 16 LLMs, covering leading frontier and open-weight models. Every model attempted all 47 puzzles in the game, plus eight community tournament puzzles, in one scored attempt each (pass@1), with 10 to 45 minutes per puzzle, depending on difficulty, to find a working program and keep improving it.
Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra lead, and the data doesn’t separate them. Both solved all 55 puzzles and both found new frontier points on 11. Opus 5.5 found more points, 72 to 32, while GPT-6 Astra has the higher record proximity, 78.0 to 77.2. Record proximity measures closeness to the community records, where 100 means matching them. The proximity gap’s 95% bootstrap interval includes zero, from −0.7 to +2.4 points. GPT-6 Astra also leads in all six tested hypervolume settings, which measure the space covered by each model’s tradeoffs.
Solving and optimizing are also different skills. Gemini 3.8 Flash solved 53 puzzles and found new points on 1; Fable 5.1 solved fewer, 52, and found new points on 5.
RL environments & traces are available upon request for research teams. Get in touch ↗
How it works: harness design
Every result here is a program we can run and test on fresh inputs, which makes a programming game a useful benchmark. Models get what a player can inspect, through text tools instead of a mouse and screenshots: the manual, visible test inputs, registers, and game feedback. They don’t get community code or exact records, only the game’s coarse score histograms.
- Read, edit, run
- Models read the puzzle and language reference, edit programs, and run them in the real game.
- Diagnostics
- Wrong outputs and deadlocks return mismatches, registers, and blocked ports, so the next edit can respond to evidence.
- Saved progress
- Every passing program joins the model’s own frontier and can be recovered with get_best, so a risky edit can’t lose an earlier result.
- Reminders
- If a model ends its turn early, a reminder asks it to keep testing, so quitting early doesn’t decide the score. Reminders contain no solution hints.
- A visible clock
- Models see time used against a 10-, 30-, or 45-minute limit. Setup doesn’t count; thinking and game calls do. Models can’t end an episode early.
- Run limits
- Game execution stops after roughly 1 second without state changes, 5 seconds without output, or 60 seconds overall, and returns diagnostics.
Why test 100,000 inputs? The game checks a small set of cases per run. Our headline count requires a fresh-game replay and 100,000 passing tests on the independent TIS-100-CXX simulator, providing stronger evidence that a program generalizes to new inputs.
One record up close
Undecimal Twin RounderSPEC44149538, one of the eight tournament puzzles, rounds an input to the nearest multiple of N on one output and of 11−N on the other. When we froze the leaderboard, the best community program took 2,694 cycles. Opus 5.5 passed its first program after 6.5 minutes, at 5,669 cycles. It went under the record 16 minutes in and finished at 1,918, which is 29% faster. That speed cost one more node and 28 more instructions than the old record.
The core of the program is a two-speed search. Instead of subtracting N one step at a time, nodes 5 and 6 subtract 4N until they overshoot, then add N back until the value turns positive. Each drives a small coprocessor, node 2 or node 7, by sending it jump offsets through a port, so the coprocessor works as a lookup table for 4N and N.
Loading puzzle trajectories…
Five models got under the old record in-game. The other two cycle records are GPT-6.1 Sol’s 3,460 on Intersection IdentifierSPEC64160260, against 3,872 (11% faster), and Gemini 4 Argon’s 188 on Error: 8SPEC79324720, against 198 (5% faster). All three are on tournament puzzles, none in the main game. Of the 133 new frontier points, 18 beat a community record outright. The other 115 are new tradeoffs: better balances between the three scores than any community solution.
What separates the models
Cost doesn’t track quality
GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 75.6 record proximity at an estimated $0.75 per puzzle. Opus 5.5 reaches 77.2 at $5.08, 7 times the cost for 2 more points. Fable 5.1 is the most expensive at $7.19 and scores 70.2.
Activity doesn’t explain quality either. GPT-6.1 Sol averages 136 game calls per puzzle at 75.6 record proximity; Gemini 4 Argon averages 41 at 76.2.
New points concentrate on hard puzzles
New frontier points appear on 14 hard puzzles, 4 medium puzzles, and no easy ones. Long-running puzzles are harder to solve but easier to improve: on puzzles with a cycle record of 200 or less, 88% of episodes pass and 4% find a new point. Above 500 cycles, 76% pass and 8% find one.
Speed is the hardest score
Every model is closest to the community on nodes and furthest on cycles. Across all 13, mean proximity is 72 for nodes, 56 for instructions, and 45 for cycles.
What the models built
We grouped all 55 puzzles by their main demand, then read the programs. Fifteen of the sixteen models solved all five routing puzzles, and none found a new frontier point there. The examples below show how different designs spend the same resources.
Multiplication: spend code to save cycles
Signal Multiplier43786 has no MUL. Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6 Astra use JRO, a relative jump, to enter a block of repeated instructions at the right position. The jump selects how many copies of a value to send and add, saving the counter updates and branches of a multiplication loop.
Gemini 4 Argon’s fastest program uses two paths to multiply in parallel and a final node to interleave their outputs. It takes 436 cycles against GPT-6 Astra’s 523, about 17% faster, at a cost of two more nodes and 33 more instructions.
Window sums: distribute the history
Signal Window Filter60099 outputs the sums of the last three and last five inputs, so a solution has to remember history as well as add. Gemini 4 Argon’s four-node program uses SWP to rotate stored values and ADD/SUB to update running state. GPT-6.1 Sol spreads that delay and aggregation across seven nodes, passing intermediate values between them.
GPT-6.1 Sol’s program runs in 318 cycles with 26 instructions; Gemini 4 Argon’s takes 428 cycles with only 17. The difference is how much of the work runs in parallel, and how much communication and code that costs.
Indexed access from stacks
T31 Node EmulatorNEXUS.23.727.9 needs eight addressable storage slots, but the available memory nodes are stacks. These programs move values between stacks to reach the requested slot, then read or replace it. MiMo-V2.6-Pro uses counted transfer loops; Opus 5.5 uses JRO to pick among unrolled transfers, spending extra instructions to save cycles.
Memory isn’t one skill: MiMo-V2.6-Pro solves this emulator but fails Sequence Mode CalculatorNEXUS.09.904.9 and Signal Window Filter60099.
Each row is that model’s fastest saved program for the puzzle, picked for illustration. Not all are new frontier points.
God mode: what if the model could see the target?
The main benchmark hides the community’s scores. In a separate study on six puzzles, five models got:
- The target: exact community scores, showing which tradeoffs remain unbeaten.
- Diagnostics: cycle-by-cycle traces and profiles of where each node stalls.
- Edge cases: a fast simulator that runs 10,000 random tests and returns failures.
- More time: 30 minutes, plus extensions for progress, up to 60.
Every model improved: GPT-6 Astra from 82.8 to 91.8, GPT-6.1 Sol from 82.9 to 90.6, Opus 5.5 from 81.4 to 89.1, Grok 4.7 from 67.5 to 75.1, and Gemini 4 Argon from 83.5 to 87.9 in mean record proximity. Scores rose in 28 of the 30 model–puzzle pairs.
The diagnostics changed what models did next. On Signal Multiplexer22280, GPT-6.1 Sol’s first passing program took 294 cycles. Its profile showed node 2 working 86% of the time while nodes 1 and 3 spent 84% blocked waiting to write to it. GPT-6.1 Sol moved the branching out of node 2 and into those two neighbors. The next run took 204 cycles, 31% faster, at a cost of two more nodes and five more instructions.
Information, tools, and time all changed together, so this study can’t say which addition helped most. These runs are outside the main leaderboard and the headline count.
Puzzles: Signal Multiplexer, Sequence Generator, Signal Edge Detector, Interrupt Handler, Sequence Peak Detector, and Signal Error Corrector.
Co-discovery
We submitted selected programs to the leaderboard, and the community improved on them almost immediately. On Undecimal Twin RounderSPEC44149538, @LongingForRest took Opus 5.5’s 1,918-cycle program and cut it to 1,744 by the next day. The record is now credited to both: LongingForRest/opus-5-5.
Neither got there alone. The models found new tradeoffs quickly, and players read those programs, worked out why they worked, and took them further.
Mathematics is seeing the same shift. Terence Tao and colleagues used LLM-guided search across 67 problems and improved on the best known results in several. In “After Math,” Silvia De Toffoli and Eamon Duede argue that a result only becomes a solution once mathematicians can understand it, and that AI fits better as an assistant than a competitor. TIS-100 is a small, measurable version of that future: a model finds a better program, and people turn it into something they understand.
Pareto explorer
Choose a puzzle and model, then select a point to see its scores and the program that produced it. Every puzzle also has its own page with records and the best programs: all 55 puzzles.
The plot shows cycles and instructions; node counts can differ. New frontier points are judged on all three scores.
Download all 3,714 model Pareto points (CSV) · all 3,714 programs (ZIP), also on GitHub and Hugging Face. 186 rows are marked as new frontier points, which pool to 133 across models.
Methods
Expand
Suite. All 22 campaign puzzles, all 25 TIS-NET puzzles, and eight tournament puzzles from 2018: 19 easy (10 minutes), 17 medium (30), and 19 hard (45). Every model has one scored episode per puzzle. Time limits differ by difficulty, so difficulty and search time can’t be separated.

articles.title: LLMs Play Zachtronics' TIS-100
articles.body:
TIS-100 Bench: LLMs Push the Pareto Frontier in Programming Puzzle Games
Twelve nodes. Two registers per node. Fifteen lines of code. In TIS-100, even multiplying two numbers is a small engineering project, and players have spent a decade optimizing these programs on a public community leaderboard. We gave 16 LLMs the game and its manual, withheld the leaderboard, and told them to keep improving.
Within days, players picked up the models’ programs and improved on most of them.
Each node is a tiny processor, and neighboring nodes have to wait for one another to exchange values. The game scores a working solution on cycles, nodes, and instructions, and you start wondering whether one more instruction could disappear. Lower is better, but improving one score can make another worse, so each puzzle has a frontier of tradeoffs instead of one best answer.
Leaderboard
We ran 16 LLMs, covering leading frontier and open-weight models. Every model attempted all 47 puzzles in the game, plus eight community tournament puzzles, in one scored attempt each (pass@1), with 10 to 45 minutes per puzzle, depending on difficulty, to find a working program and keep improving it.
Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra lead, and the data doesn’t separate them. Both solved all 55 puzzles and both found new frontier points on 11. Opus 5.5 found more points, 72 to 32, while GPT-6 Astra has the higher record proximity, 78.0 to 77.2. Record proximity measures closeness to the community records, where 100 means matching them. The proximity gap’s 95% bootstrap interval includes zero, from −0.7 to +2.4 points. GPT-6 Astra also leads in all six tested hypervolume settings, which measure the space covered by each model’s tradeoffs.
Solving and optimizing are also different skills. Gemini 3.8 Flash solved 53 puzzles and found new points on 1; Fable 5.1 solved fewer, 52, and found new points on 5.
RL environments & traces are available upon request for research teams. Get in touch ↗
How it works: harness design
Every result here is a program we can run and test on fresh inputs, which makes a programming game a useful benchmark. Models get what a player can inspect, through text tools instead of a mouse and screenshots: the manual, visible test inputs, registers, and game feedback. They don’t get community code or exact records, only the game’s coarse score histograms.
- Read, edit, run
- Models read the puzzle and language reference, edit programs, and run them in the real game.
- Diagnostics
- Wrong outputs and deadlocks return mismatches, registers, and blocked ports, so the next edit can respond to evidence.
- Saved progress
- Every passing program joins the model’s own frontier and can be recovered with get_best, so a risky edit can’t lose an earlier result.
- Reminders
- If a model ends its turn early, a reminder asks it to keep testing, so quitting early doesn’t decide the score. Reminders contain no solution hints.
- A visible clock
- Models see time used against a 10-, 30-, or 45-minute limit. Setup doesn’t count; thinking and game calls do. Models can’t end an episode early.
- Run limits
- Game execution stops after roughly 1 second without state changes, 5 seconds without output, or 60 seconds overall, and returns diagnostics.
Why test 100,000 inputs? The game checks a small set of cases per run. Our headline count requires a fresh-game replay and 100,000 passing tests on the independent TIS-100-CXX simulator, providing stronger evidence that a program generalizes to new inputs.
One record up close
Undecimal Twin RounderSPEC44149538, one of the eight tournament puzzles, rounds an input to the nearest multiple of N on one output and of 11−N on the other. When we froze the leaderboard, the best community program took 2,694 cycles. Opus 5.5 passed its first program after 6.5 minutes, at 5,669 cycles. It went under the record 16 minutes in and finished at 1,918, which is 29% faster. That speed cost one more node and 28 more instructions than the old record.
The core of the program is a two-speed search. Instead of subtracting N one step at a time, nodes 5 and 6 subtract 4N until they overshoot, then add N back until the value turns positive. Each drives a small coprocessor, node 2 or node 7, by sending it jump offsets through a port, so the coprocessor works as a lookup table for 4N and N.
Loading puzzle trajectories…
Five models got under the old record in-game. The other two cycle records are GPT-6.1 Sol’s 3,460 on Intersection IdentifierSPEC64160260, against 3,872 (11% faster), and Gemini 4 Argon’s 188 on Error: 8SPEC79324720, against 198 (5% faster). All three are on tournament puzzles, none in the main game. Of the 133 new frontier points, 18 beat a community record outright. The other 115 are new tradeoffs: better balances between the three scores than any community solution.
What separates the models
Cost doesn’t track quality
GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 75.6 record proximity at an estimated $0.75 per puzzle. Opus 5.5 reaches 77.2 at $5.08, 7 times the cost for 2 more points. Fable 5.1 is the most expensive at $7.19 and scores 70.2.
Activity doesn’t explain quality either. GPT-6.1 Sol averages 136 game calls per puzzle at 75.6 record proximity; Gemini 4 Argon averages 41 at 76.2.
New points concentrate on hard puzzles
New frontier points appear on 14 hard puzzles, 4 medium puzzles, and no easy ones. Long-running puzzles are harder to solve but easier to improve: on puzzles with a cycle record of 200 or less, 88% of episodes pass and 4% find a new point. Above 500 cycles, 76% pass and 8% find one.
Speed is the hardest score
Every model is closest to the community on nodes and furthest on cycles. Across all 13, mean proximity is 72 for nodes, 56 for instructions, and 45 for cycles.
What the models built
We grouped all 55 puzzles by their main demand, then read the programs. Fifteen of the sixteen models solved all five routing puzzles, and none found a new frontier point there. The examples below show how different designs spend the same resources.
Multiplication: spend code to save cycles
Signal Multiplier43786 has no MUL. Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6 Astra use JRO, a relative jump, to enter a block of repeated instructions at the right position. The jump selects how many copies of a value to send and add, saving the counter updates and branches of a multiplication loop.
Gemini 4 Argon’s fastest program uses two paths to multiply in parallel and a final node to interleave their outputs. It takes 436 cycles against GPT-6 Astra’s 523, about 17% faster, at a cost of two more nodes and 33 more instructions.
Window sums: distribute the history
Signal Window Filter60099 outputs the sums of the last three and last five inputs, so a solution has to remember history as well as add. Gemini 4 Argon’s four-node program uses SWP to rotate stored values and ADD/SUB to update running state. GPT-6.1 Sol spreads that delay and aggregation across seven nodes, passing intermediate values between them.
GPT-6.1 Sol’s program runs in 318 cycles with 26 instructions; Gemini 4 Argon’s takes 428 cycles with only 17. The difference is how much of the work runs in parallel, and how much communication and code that costs.
Indexed access from stacks
T31 Node EmulatorNEXUS.23.727.9 needs eight addressable storage slots, but the available memory nodes are stacks. These programs move values between stacks to reach the requested slot, then read or replace it. MiMo-V2.6-Pro uses counted transfer loops; Opus 5.5 uses JRO to pick among unrolled transfers, spending extra instructions to save cycles.
Memory isn’t one skill: MiMo-V2.6-Pro solves this emulator but fails Sequence Mode CalculatorNEXUS.09.904.9 and Signal Window Filter60099.
Each row is that model’s fastest saved program for the puzzle, picked for illustration. Not all are new frontier points.
God mode: what if the model could see the target?
The main benchmark hides the community’s scores. In a separate study on six puzzles, five models got:
- The target: exact community scores, showing which tradeoffs remain unbeaten.
- Diagnostics: cycle-by-cycle traces and profiles of where each node stalls.
- Edge cases: a fast simulator that runs 10,000 random tests and returns failures.
- More time: 30 minutes, plus extensions for progress, up to 60.
Every model improved: GPT-6 Astra from 82.8 to 91.8, GPT-6.1 Sol from 82.9 to 90.6, Opus 5.5 from 81.4 to 89.1, Grok 4.7 from 67.5 to 75.1, and Gemini 4 Argon from 83.5 to 87.9 in mean record proximity. Scores rose in 28 of the 30 model–puzzle pairs.
The diagnostics changed what models did next. On Signal Multiplexer22280, GPT-6.1 Sol’s first passing program took 294 cycles. Its profile showed node 2 working 86% of the time while nodes 1 and 3 spent 84% blocked waiting to write to it. GPT-6.1 Sol moved the branching out of node 2 and into those two neighbors. The next run took 204 cycles, 31% faster, at a cost of two more nodes and five more instructions.
Information, tools, and time all changed together, so this study can’t say which addition helped most. These runs are outside the main leaderboard and the headline count.
Puzzles: Signal Multiplexer, Sequence Generator, Signal Edge Detector, Interrupt Handler, Sequence Peak Detector, and Signal Error Corrector.
Co-discovery
We submitted selected programs to the leaderboard, and the community improved on them almost immediately. On Undecimal Twin RounderSPEC44149538, @LongingForRest took Opus 5.5’s 1,918-cycle program and cut it to 1,744 by the next day. The record is now credited to both: LongingForRest/opus-5-5.
Neither got there alone. The models found new tradeoffs quickly, and players read those programs, worked out why they worked, and took them further.
Mathematics is seeing the same shift. Terence Tao and colleagues used LLM-guided search across 67 problems and improved on the best known results in several. In “After Math,” Silvia De Toffoli and Eamon Duede argue that a result only becomes a solution once mathematicians can understand it, and that AI fits better as an assistant than a competitor. TIS-100 is a small, measurable version of that future: a model finds a better program, and people turn it into something they understand.
Pareto explorer
Choose a puzzle and model, then select a point to see its scores and the program that produced it. Every puzzle also has its own page with records and the best programs: all 55 puzzles.
The plot shows cycles and instructions; node counts can differ. New frontier points are judged on all three scores.
Download all 3,714 model Pareto points (CSV) · all 3,714 programs (ZIP), also on GitHub and Hugging Face. 186 rows are marked as new frontier points, which pool to 133 across models.

articles.title: $30M Raised to Redo the CPU
articles.body:
$30M Raised to Redo the CPU
As of today, Tendrils has completed a $30M round led by Benchmark to rebuild general-purpose computing.
Contemporary CPUs are made under the constraint of backwards compatibility with sequential, single-core chips. Accumulated layers of historical designs are locking engineers into decisions dating back to the 1970s. As a result, all existing CPUs are bottlenecked by complex cache coherency protocols and elaborate reorder buffers. CPU scaling is sabotaged from the start. At Tendrils, we believe that the future of general-purpose computing lies beyond legacy architectures for legacy software.
Tendrils is answering the question: what if we redo the CPU? Instead of starting from a sequential design, we’re building our processor to have thousands of cores operating in parallel. This requires moving beyond the notion of shared mutable memory and linear instruction sequences. To make this possible, we’re working in tandem on the open-source language Vine, which has been designed from the beginning to target a new wave of parallel-first architectures.
We’re delighted to announce that Tendrils has raised $30 million to support this vision. This round is led by Benchmark, with significant participation from Visionaries Club, the UK Sovereign AI Fund, FR8, Antimatter, Cloudberry VC, Conviction, Embassy Ventures, and SV Angels. We are grateful for additional support provided by all of our angel investors. Additionally, we wish to extend a warm welcome to our newest board member, Jack Altman.
With thanks to all who have supported us,
The Tendrils Team
At Tendrils, we insist that the chips of the future will be a result of close collaboration between hardware and software engineers. If this strikes you, consider joining us.

articles.title: Ember’s latest self-heating 14-ounce mug is $50 off
articles.body:
If you were cool on the $149.95 original price of the 14-ounce Ember Mug 3, you might warm up to the current discount happening at Amazon, Ember, and Best Buy for several colors of the (top rack) dishwasher-safe mug. It’s 33 percent off, dropping to $99.99 — still not cheap, but cheaper, and notably just $10 more than the 10-ounce version.
Ember’s latest self-heating 14-ounce mug is $50 off
A great deal on a dishwasher-safe mug that stays hot. We also found discounts on Blu-rays and self-coiling USB-C cables.
The Mug 3 affords you a couple of ways to control your drink’s temperature. A power button on the bottom of the mug can cycle between five temperature presets (125 to 145 degrees Fahrenheit), or you can use the app. It includes a sipping lid, and Ember claims that the Mug 3’s battery can keep drinks hot for up to three hours with the lid on. Without it, drinks stay hot for 80 minutes, the same battery claim as the Mug 2.
As we inch closer to the gift-getting season, the Ember Mug 3 seems like a solid product to snag for a coffee or tea lover who works from home, or for parents who have their hands full with kids and could always use a cuppa.
Some more great Verge-approved deals
- Criterion Collection DVDs and Blu-rays are half off through December 6th at Amazon and Barnes and Noble, meaning you have plenty of time to assemble a wishlist of movies you want to buy ahead of the holiday season. The company’s catalog of films is vast, and it’s the best place to get limited edition releases of cherished films, old and new. Some of Criterion’s recent physical releases have been a hit, especially because they’ve quickly sunk in price. KPop Demon Hunters on 4K Blu-ray is just $24.99 at Amazon and Barnes and Noble. Also, The Complete Kubrick boxset (currently the only way to get 4K Blu-ray versions of every one of the director’s legendary films) is half off, too, down to $299.99.
- I’ve been wanting a USB-C cable that coils itself magnetically since my colleague Sean Hollister wrote about his favorites last year. That said, they tend to be a little pricey even if their tech specs are similar to cheaper cables, mostly due to the party trick. However, Werewolf (the company that makes the clever VFLEX for powering older gadgets via a USB-C power bank or wall charger) makes its own six-foot magnetic USB-C cable that’s just $12 right now (originally $27.50). It’s braided and supports up to 240W power passthrough, so it meets my criteria.
- Google’s Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch is $100 off in both the Wi-Fi and LTE configurations at Amazon, though not all colors are included in the discount. The most affordable (and smallest) option is the 41mm Wi-Fi Pixel Watch 5, which costs $299.99. The larger 45mm watch face adds $30 to the price tag compared to the smaller version, whether you want Wi-Fi or LTE. One of the biggest improvements made to this generation is its GPS tracking. Google claims that it can outperform the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro — both of which cost a lot more — and we were impressed during our hands-on testing. Victoria Song tested it in the signal-congested West Village in Manhattan, walking in zigzags in an attempt to throw off the tracking. It wasn’t perfect, but it more accurately tracked turn-by-turn movement better than the Ultra 3. Read our review.

articles.title: M John Harrison Becomes First Sci-Fi Author To Win Booker Prize
articles.body:
M John Harrison Becomes First Sci-Fi Author To Win Booker Prize (theguardian.com) 16
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award's history. Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison's was "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world." She called it "a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page".
Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the 50,000-pound award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening. The End of Everything, Harrison's first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist.
Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. "It's a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile -- and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism," she said. "One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won't matter either  This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future."

articles.title: New York Launches Nation's First State AI Testing Program
articles.body:
New York Launches Nation's First State AI Testing Program (politico.com) 17
			
		 	
				New York is launching a state-backed AI safety research center at Binghamton University that will independently study and test AI systems, develop safety and security techniques, and train researchers in responsible AI. "While the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said. "The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word." Politico reports:  The center -- which is funded by a $30 million gift from Bloomberg co-founder Tom Secunda and a $25 million research investment from SUNY and New York state -- is set to launch before New York's major AI safety law, the RAISE Act, comes into effect on Jan. 1. That will require submissions of detailed safety frameworks from AI companies operating in New York State, which Hochul's office hopes will be scrutinized by researchers at the new center.
"AI is opening up questions that scientists could not tackle before," said Secunda, who also serves as the board chair of Empire AI, a $500 million public-private partnership. "With Empire AI and researchers across New York, the Center can test systems independently and give public officials evidence they can use."
Over 80 leading scientists and researchers on AI systems from across New York state will contribute to the effort, which will be run by the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, according to details shared by Hochul's office. The initiative will be led by Jeannette Wing, the executive vice president for research at Columbia University, and Greg Morrisett, the vice provost of Cornell Tech.
"We need new techniques that can be applied to this new kind of system with swarms of autonomous agents acting independently and without control. How can you first detect that they're going to do harm, and how can you prevent them from doing harm?" said Wing. "The beauty of what's being proposed is that this state is committing resources to really light this up."

articles.title: Nintendo Is Officially Investing In Game Preservation
articles.body:
Nintendo Is Officially Investing In Game Preservation 28
			
		 	
				Nintendo is hiring a digital archivist to help ensure the company's historical records are "preserved for future generations." The 12-month position is tasked with designing and implementing a "structured framework for organizing technical records, engineering documentation, source materials, and institutional knowledge related to legacy systems and platforms." Polygon reports:  In the past, Nintendo has drawn criticism from the preservation community. In 2022, the Video Game History Foundation publicly criticized the company for announcing it would be closing the Wii U and 3DS eShops. The foundation released a statement saying that Nintendo's decision was "actively destructive to video game history." The statement also pointed out that Nintendo is part of the Entertainment Software Association, which funds lobbying that prevents a number of preservation efforts.

articles.title: Physically Controllable Relighting of Photographs
articles.body:
We present a photograph relighting method that enables explicit control over light sources akin to CG pipelines. Users can insert different types of light sources, such as spot lights, point lights, or environmental illumination into the scene. We achieve this in a pipeline involving mid-level computer vision, physically-based rendering, and neural rendering. We introduce a self-supervised training methodology using differentiable rendering to train our neural renderer with real-world photograph collections for in-the-wild generalization.
Abstract
We present a self-supervised approach to in-the-wild image relighting that enables fully controllable, physically based illumination editing.
We achieve this by combining the physical accuracy of traditional rendering with the photorealistic appearance made possible by neural rendering.
Our pipeline works by inferring a colored mesh representation of a given scene using monocular estimates of geometry and intrinsic components.
This representation allows users to define their desired illumination configuration in 3D. The scene under the new lighting can then be rendered using a path-tracing engine.
We send this approximate rendering of the scene through a feed-forward neural renderer to predict the final photorealistic relighting result.
We develop a differentiable rendering process to reconstruct in-the-wild scene illumination, enabling self-supervised training of our neural renderer on raw image collections.
Our method represents a significant step in bringing the explicit physical control over lights available in typical 3D computer graphics tools, such as Blender, to in-the-wild relighting.

articles.title: The Zig project is going nowhere
articles.body:
Zig keeps improving as a programming language. Unfortunately, its management increasingly seems determined to make it a bad choice for the people who actually want to use it.
Zig is a fascinating programming language. Its design contains genuinely good ideas, its technical ambitions are impressive, and it has attracted talented developers who have spent years building a serious systems programming toolchain. And despite all that, it's becoming increasingly hard to recommend it.
The problem is that Zig appears to be poorly managed.
Over the past year, the project has made a series of decisions that individually might seem like ordinary disagreements about open-source development, while together revealing a deeply concerning pattern.
The language continues to break compatibility without a concrete commitment to stability. Its contribution policy excludes otherwise legitimate engineering workflows. One of its most prominent users abandoned the language, only to be met with public hostility. And its move away from GitHub replaced a mature development platform with a smaller, less proven service beset with reliability issues, whose operators increasingly impose their own philosophical preferences on hosted projects.
The recurring theme is that Zig's maintainers appear more interested in enforcing their vision of how software should be developed than making Zig a practical tool for people who want to build software. And that is a serious problem for a programming language.
Zig is perpetually unfinished, and its users pay the price
Zig has been under development for more than a decade. It remains at version 0.x, without a firm date for a stable 1.0 release.
There is nothing inherently wrong with a long development cycle or a version number below 1.0. Plenty of useful software operates under so-called 0ver. esbuild is one prominent example of rock-solid, uncompromising quality and little breakage despite its major version remaining at 0.
But Zig is a programming language, not a bundler.
A programming language is infrastructure. Developers write applications and libraries against its syntax, standard library, compiler, and build tooling, and those interfaces determine how much of the surrounding ecosystem remains usable from one release to the next. In Zig, they seem to be forever changing, with the authors nigh-obsessed about breakage.
Consider the 0.15.1 release notes, with substantial changes to the I/O interfaces and standard library, including the lovingly named ‘Writergate’. It's amusing enough if you're writing the compiler, presumably less if you're the one whose code no longer compiles. Other participants raised much the same concern, with one arguing that Codeberg hadn't yet matured enough to be relied on as a serious GitHub replacement.

After acknowledging how important the platform had been to Zig's fundraising, the maintainers wrote:
"Although GitHub Sponsors is a large fraction of Zig Software Foundation’s donation income, we consider it a liability."

Why should people who are already supporting Zig have to change their payment arrangements just because the maintainers no longer like GitHub? The actual development could happen entirely on Codeberg. Nobody would have to use GitHub for issues, pull requests, or CI. And the people who prefer GitHub Sponsors could continue donating through it.
Perhaps there were administrative reasons for wanting to consolidate fundraising elsewhere. But the announcement doesn't establish why keeping both channels was unacceptable. The maintainers did thank their existing supporters, and they weren't literally refusing donations. But I still find the message remarkably tone-deaf.
When your project relies on voluntary contributions, making it less convenient for people to support you should require a better explanation than disliking the platform they happen to use.
It's one thing to refuse to depend on GitHub for development. It's another to turn that preference into unnecessary friction for people who are trying to give you money.
Once again, everyone else is expected to accommodate Zig's principles.
Going nowhere
Zig isn't dead. Development continues, and the compiler keeps getting better.
But technical progress isn't the same thing as maturity. What good is an increasingly sophisticated programming language if using it remains an exercise in keeping up with breaking changes and the whims of project management?
Look at the pattern. Users are expected to keep up with an unstable language. Contributors are expected to work the approved way. A prominent downstream user decides Rust fits better, and the project publicly lashes out. The hosting platform changes, and donors are asked to move along with it.

A developer wants to write software, not spend countless hours migrating standard-library APIs. A contributor might want to fix a bug, not prove allegiance to a sanctioned school of engineering. A company wants a language that solves its problems, not a lecture about how to run its business. And a donor wants to support a project, not get embroiled in its dispute with GitHub.

Sometimes it means accepting a useful patch from someone who doesn't share your preferred development ideology. Sometimes it means swallowing your pride when a major user moves on. And sometimes it means choosing boring, reliable infrastructure instead of making a philosophical statement.
Zig seems determined to do anything but that.
None of this is inevitable. Zig could keep its technical ambitions while becoming a much more dependable language and a much easier project to work with. But that would require its maintainers to start treating users' needs as something more than an inconvenience to be managed.
The project can keep refining its language design forever. It can keep insisting on its own idea of good engineering, rejecting the wrong kinds of contributions, and choosing platforms that align with its worldview.
But at some point, it needs to decide whether it wants to build a programming language people can use or an ongoing experiment in how its maintainers think software should be developed.
Zig has spent more than a decade figuring out what its maintainers want the language to be. Perhaps it's time they started caring a little more about what its users need it to be.
Until then, the Zig project is going nowhere.

articles.body:
Call of Duty: Black Ops II, statically recompiled from 32-bit x86 Windows to native ARM64 macOS.
Campaign, Zombies and multiplayer against bots, built on your Mac from your own Steam copy.
English · 中文
Why · Abstract · Method · Limits · Repository · Legal
Beta, 2026-11-03 · measured on one Apple M1 (4 performance + 4 efficiency cores, 16 GB)
Campaign (Angola), Zombies (Town) and multiplayer (Hijacked, against bots) on an Apple M1, recorded while playing; the number in the top right corner is frames per second, and the screen recording itself costs some, mostly in the campaign. 80-second video (MP4, 20 MB)
Important
This repository contains no game file and no translated game code. It turns your own Steam copy of Black Ops II into an app for your Mac, on your Mac. The game's code ends up inside that app, so nobody can hand you a ready-made one: each player builds their own, and it may not be shared. Unofficial fan project, not affiliated with Activision, Treyarch or Microsoft. To play, buy the game. Beta: read what has and has not been proven.
Black Ops II never came out on Mac, and on Apple Silicon it was not really playable before. AppleGamingWiki lists it as unplayable under CrossOver and not supported under Rosetta 2. What remains is a Windows ARM virtual machine in Parallels, with reports ranging from 1 frame per second in matches on an M1 Max to 60–80 on M3 and M4 (MacGamingDB). Here the game is translated once, before it starts, into a native ARM64 app: 51–60 frames per second on a base M1, with no Windows and no virtual machine. Being native also means it can be fixed and extended like any Mac app: split-screen, which the PC version never had, is in progress.
bo2-mac takes the three executables of Black Ops II, the campaign (t6sp.exe), Zombies (t6zm.exe) and
multiplayer (t6mp.exe), and turns their x86 machine code into ARM64 machine code ahead of time.
Remill lifts each function to LLVM IR, a chain of our own passes rewrites
that IR, and the result is linked with a Win32 runtime written by hand, whose Direct3D 11 is drawn by Metal. There is
no Wine and no JIT: the game runs as native code, in one process. About 150,000 functions are translated across the
three executables. Only the short sequences that the copy protection hides run in a small x86 interpreter, and so does
any code the translation missed, so a hole is built to cost speed rather than crash the game.
On an Apple M1 the campaign runs at 51–60 frames per second, and every mission loads and hands over to the next
one, down to the end credits. Zombies is played solo on six maps through the game's own menus at 57–60.
Multiplayer is played against bots through its real menus, eleven game modes, at 53–60. One app,
Black Ops II.app, opens the campaign, and the CAMPAIGN / ZOMBIES / MULTIPLAYER entries of each menu switch to the
other game.
Nothing is downloaded from anyone but you: the converter reads the executables of the copy you bought, checks them byte for byte, and builds the app on your machine.
Frame rate counts the drawables really presented to the screen, checked against the screen and the Metal HUD.
What you can play
All three modes: keyboard and mouse, or a DualSense as XInput through GameController.framework; sound on; movement keys follow their position on your keyboard (ZQSD on AZERTY, WASD on QWERTY), unless you bound them yourself in the game's options.
In five steps, all on the player's Mac:
- Check. The converter accepts only the exact Steam build of each executable, checked by SHA-256. The launcher asks the Steam client on your Mac whether the signed-in account owns the game, and refuses otherwise.
- Catalogue and lift. Ghidra lists the functions of your own executable; Remill v6.0.1 lifts each one to LLVM IR. Five patches to the lifter are carried in tools/remill-patches/, among them the x87 rounding mode, and one that forks a running Remill for each function instead of reloading its x86 semantics.
- Fold. Remill's IR is correct but slow: every guest memory access, flag and x87 push is a call or a store
into a State structure. Our passes rewrite it before clang -O2: guest reads and writes are inlined, lock sequences become hardware atomics, the guest ret stays inside the lifted code, and the x87 stack is promoted to
locals.
- Runtime. runtime/ implements the Windows imports the game really calls, with exact stdcall arities (the Steam API ones taken from Valve's public headers). Guest memory is one 4 GiB mapping. Direct3D 11 is a fake-COM layer over Metal; DXBC shaders go through HLSLcc. XAudio2 goes to CoreAudio, and the videos are decoded natively with libvpx.
- Threads. Guest threads start as coroutines on one host thread, which removes most sources of non-determinism and makes a run replayable. The fast configuration moves the server, the render backend, sound mixing and decoding, and the job workers onto real host threads. ARM is not TSO, so this needed real memory barriers.
The copy protection is executed, not bypassed. The game hides integrity checks behind hardware exceptions, single-step traps and code it decrypts into the heap. A small x86 machine built on Unicorn (x86_guest_vm.cpp, heap_code.cpp) runs exactly those sequences and hands control back to the recompiled code. No check result is forced and no key is placed by hand.
A hole in the translation is built to cost speed, not a crash. When the game reaches x86 code that was never lifted, the
same machine runs its original bytes (interp.cpp) and gives control back to the
recompiled code at the next translated block, call or return. Each interpreted address is logged ([INTERP]).
The online service is answered locally. Zombies and multiplayer expect Demonware; a responder written from the game's own requests (dw_local.cpp) answers the lobby, storage and ticket on your Mac. Nothing leaves the machine.
Why not Wine, CrossOver, DXVK or DXMT?
They translate Windows calls at run time and keep the x86 code under Rosetta. Here the x86 code itself is gone: it is ARM64 machine code before the game starts. DXVK and DXMT are PE DLLs that reach their native backend through Wine's unixlib mechanism; this port has no Wine, and its Direct3D 11 is its own layer over 32-bit guest memory. Only shader translation was needed from outside, and HLSLcc, a plain C++ library, covers it.
Each entry is a symptom seen on screen, the cause that was measured, and the effect of the fix.
Thirteen findings, from the x87 rounding mode to a false start inside one instruction
F1 · The lifter ignored the x87 rounding mode. In Zombies the prone view shook. fistp rounded to nearest where
the game had asked for truncation, inside the network codec of the view height. The height received by the client was
wrong on 8 samples out of 8, and on 0 out of 8 after a Remill patch and a re-lift of the codec.
F2 · One reserved bit of the x87 control word. A campaign mission froze in an effects loop, only with real threads. The lifter stored bit 6 of the control word differently from real hardware. A one-line Remill patch and four re-lifted runtime functions fixed it, with no slowdown.
F3 · A CPU feature flag changes the algorithm. Our IsProcessorFeaturePresent answered "no SSE2", so the C
runtime took its x87 ceil, which rounded to nearest under our runtime. An effect then sampled index −1 forever: two
missions froze.
F4 · Our own log caused the stutter. Hitches of 170–430 ms were the render thread blocked in write(): our log,
redirected to a file on a nearly full disk. Sending it through a pipe to a child process took the hitches per run from
12 and 8 to 0 and 0.
F5 · Shader translation moved constants by 4 bytes. HLSLcc placed a float2 after a float at offset 24 where
Direct3D reads it at 20. 31 of 2,664 shaders were affected, among them the eyes and the reticles.
F6 · The protection has to run. The options menu froze 8 times out of 8. An integrity check rewrites its own return address to point at code decrypted into the heap, which the runtime ignored. Running that code, as Windows does, gave 3 out of 3 without a freeze.
F7 · Our own safety guards were the obstacle. One guard of ours stopped the game at 28 seconds of play. The largest gains of the project came from removing our own guards and false sharing, not from clever code.
F8 · An empty API stub looks like a broken service. Two stubs that returned nothing (CryptGenRandom,
StringFromGUID2) looked like a network failure in Zombies.
F9 · Thread priorities are part of the program. SetThreadPriority was a stub. Passing the mixer's request to
macOS cut the short audio buffers of a run from 908–1872 to 7–71, and the sound gaps with them.
F10 · Native skinning, bit for bit. CPU skinning rewritten in NEON gives the same bits as the original x86 and took a heavy scene from 17.8 to 30.3 fps.
F11 · Decals need the game's depth bias. Scorch marks and blood appeared or vanished with a slight turn of the camera. The game asks for a depth bias on decals; our layer left it at zero. Passing the game's values to Metal fixed it.
F12 · The render thread was copying the level's geometry every frame. In multiplayer and Zombies it copied 23–63 MB of vertex data to the GPU per frame, most of it static. Keeping static buffers resident in Metal brought the copies to 3.5–5 MB per frame: multiplayer 51.8 → 60 fps, Zombies 43.1 → 58.2. The same change does nothing in the campaign, where the pace is set by the scheduler thread. A speed-up helps only the mode whose bottleneck it touches.
F13 · A false start inside one instruction cost half the frame rate in combat. In the first conversions from a fresh Steam copy, Zombies fell to 25 fps whenever the player fired. Hot functions were running in the interpreter: the catalogue placed the start of the next function inside the first instruction of a root, so its bounded sweep decoded zero bytes and the root was dropped without a word. Sweeping such roots without the bound, as the one-by-one lifter already did, put them back in the translated code.
Predict, then measure.
- A prediction is written before the result is read: about 1,100 numbered ones by the time of this beta.
- At least three runs per configuration. Run-to-run noise is 30–64%, so a difference under about 40% cannot be seen at n = 3.
- A change must prove it is active: the log has to show it firing.
- A run that never reaches the level is a dead run, not a data point.
- The screen beats the log. When the screen contradicts a probe, the probe is wrong.
Record and replay, retractions, clean room, who does what
Deterministic record and replay. With every guest thread a coroutine on one host thread, most sources of non-determinism are gone; the replay is checked against the recording, not assumed. Three boundaries capture all outside input: the import dispatcher, the window message drain, and the consumed audio buffers. The journal is about 16 MB. It allows the same run twice with exactly one flag changed.
The instrument is the thing that fails. Nearly 200 findings were taken back along the way. The largest share (31%) were an instrument that answered a different question; the next (17%), one that could not answer at all. So every oracle here names its input and refuses to answer when that input is missing.
Clean room for the match rules. Multiplayer and Zombies take their match rules from a daily patch file that Steam no longer ships. The replacement in runtime/match_rules/ was written by a team that never saw the original script: one team wrote a behavioural specification from the game, the other wrote the code from that specification alone, and the two only spoke through written questions and answers, kept with their dates.
Who does what. AI agents supply the throughput: writing the shims, bisecting millions of calls per run, reading tens of thousands of lines. The human supplies the goal, the corrections from what is really on screen, and refuses the flattering conclusion. This is one game, months of work and heavy manual intervention.
- Local only. Multiplayer and Zombies run against the responder on your Mac. There is no online play, no LAN and no co-op yet. League Play is refused.
- Match rules are ours. Written in a clean room (see Method); behaviour may differ from the original in places.
- Heat. The Mac runs very hot during long sessions (111–116 °C reported on the M1). Play plugged in: on battery, macOS throttles the game hard. Plugging in avoids the slowdown, not the heat.
- First game on each map. In Zombies and multiplayer, shaders are translated for Metal while the map loads, so that first load is longer and the first minute can still hitch slightly. In the campaign they are translated when they first appear, so the loading cinematic stays smooth and the first pass through a place can hitch. Everything is cached: the next time, it loads fast and runs smooth.
- Window. The game runs in a 1280×720 window.
- Other Macs. Only one M1 has been measured. M2, M3 and M4 should be faster, but no number is claimed.
- Campaign. Every mission loads and chains; not every one has been played end to end.
- Zombies. Grief and Turned need a second player, and there is no co-op yet.
- macOS audio. When the system's coreaudiod is unhealthy the campaign stalls on its first video. Check that afplay -t 1 /System/Library/Sounds/Tink.aiff takes about 1 s; restarting the Mac fixes it.
You need an Apple silicon Mac, macOS 14 or later, at least 20 GB free (the conversion peaks at about 10 GB and about 4 GB stays), Homebrew, and Steam for Mac signed in to the account that owns the game.
git clone https://github.com/adrbn/bo2-mac.git && cd bo2-mac
brew install llvm@17 cmake ninja libvpx unicorn
pip3 install capstone
scripts/make_app.sh --from-source
Open Black Ops II.app, point it at your game folder and let it convert: about 1 hour 45 on an M1, the campaign first in about 45 minutes. The campaign is
playable as soon as it is converted: play it then, and Zombies and multiplayer are converted when you first pick them
in the game's menu. Otherwise the conversion goes on through all three. If the disk falls under
8 GB free, the conversion stops cleanly and resumes where it was.
Updating, or if the conversion stops. Run git pull && scripts/make_app.sh --from-source in the repository
folder: what is already converted is kept and the conversion resumes. An update redoes only what its changes touch: a
fix to the runtime relinks the three modes in about 3 minutes on an M1 instead of converting again. If it still fails,
open an issue with the log it names.
The converter only accepts the exact Steam build, checked by SHA-256. The Steam executables are encrypted by Valve's
SteamStub wrapper and this repository provides no way to remove it: the converter expects the three decrypted
images in ~/.bo2-native/steam/ (t6sp.exe.unpacked.exe, t6mp.exe.unpacked.exe, t6zm.exe.unpacked.exe). You make
them yourself from the copy you bought, with a separate tool of your choice. Only the wrapper must go: the file names
above and the SHA-256 check tell you at once whether a file is right. Never share these files.
DLC. The launcher asks your Steam client which DLC your account owns, exactly as the game does on Windows. A DLC map plays when you own it and its files are in your game folder.
- This beta: the three modes from a fresh Steam copy, on other Macs than the one that built them. Your reports (Mac model, frame rate, what broke) decide what comes next. First outside report, 2026-11-05: on an M2 Pro (16 GB), the conversion completed and the game started, after three fixes found on the way (#4, #5, #6).
- No Terminal: one app to download and open, then drop the game folder on its window. It carries its tools already built, so nothing is compiled on your Mac but the game itself (macOS 26 or later; macOS 14 and 15 keep the Terminal install).
- Fully translated: the 46 code blocks that still run through the Unicorn interpreter are translated ahead of time, and every translated instruction is checked against the interpreter; any translated function can be sent back to the interpreter, to find a wrong one by halving.
- No shader wait: shaders built before the first match, instead of at launch (about 3 minutes in multiplayer) and during play (freezes when a new effect appears). Started: shaders now compile in batches, and the ones from the last sessions compile in the background at launch. In multiplayer on an M1 without Xcode (a few tries, not a benchmark), shader compiling during the first two minutes of a match went from 18–25 s to 10–14 s on a first launch and about 5 s on the next one; freezes over 300 ms went from 15–22 to 13–15, then 7. The first launch still freezes about as often.
- Shorter conversion: down from about 2.5 hours to 1 hour 45 on an M1 (2026-11-06, measured on all three modes: the preparation reads the executable once, the lift and the fold use every core the memory allows). An update now redoes only what changed (a runtime fix: about 3 minutes). Next: less optimisation for code that rarely runs. The three modes share only 4 % of their functions, so converting shared code once would gain little.
- Faster, without heat: the campaign is bound by the scheduler thread, not by rendering; multiplayer with 11 bots is bound by the server thread. Native rewrites of the hottest functions come next, then frame rates above 60 for 120 Hz screens.
- Controllers: vibration and aim assist.
- Together: real UDP sockets for Zombies co-op, Grief and Turned, and multiplayer over LAN. Then local split screen, which the PC version never had: two copies of the game drawn in one window, one controller each, joined over that LAN.
- Later: MetalFX, post-processing when the frame is presented, and replacement textures loaded from the player's own copy.
For a copy the user owns, on hardware the user owns.
- No engine source and no leaked code are used.
- Neither the input binary nor the recompiled output is distributed. No game file is included: the player needs their own Steam copy of Call of Duty: Black Ops II. The converter only accepts the exact Steam build (SHA-256), and ownership is checked each time the game starts by the player's own Steam client: the game refuses to run when Steam is not signed in or the account does not own it.
- The copy protection is executed as the game wrote it; nothing in it is patched out. This repository provides no way to remove Valve's SteamStub wrapper.
- The online service the game expects is answered by a local responder written from the game's own requests: no Activision server is contacted, there is no online play, and game ownership is still checked by the player's Steam. The match rules were written in a clean room.
- The code written here is licensed under GPL-3.0 (LICENSE).
- Unicorn (GPL-2.0) is linked statically from Homebrew when you build (tools/boot.py). GPL-2.0 and GPL-3.0 code cannot be shipped together in one binary, so the prebuilt tools of roadmap step 2 cannot embed Unicorn as it is linked today. Building from source on your own Mac is not affected.
This is an unofficial fan project. Call of Duty and Black Ops are trademarks of Activision Publishing, Inc. Steam is a trademark of Valve Corporation. This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Activision, Treyarch, Microsoft or Valve. To play, buy the game.
