- Heat. The Mac runs very hot during long sessions (111–116 °C reported on the M1). Play plugged in: on battery, macOS throttles the game hard. Plugging in avoids the slowdown, not the heat.
- First game on each map. In Zombies and multiplayer, shaders are translated for Metal while the map loads, so that first load is longer and the first minute can still hitch slightly. In the campaign they are translated when they first appear, so the loading cinematic stays smooth and the first pass through a place can hitch. Everything is cached: the next time, it loads fast and runs smooth.
- Window. The game runs in a 1280×720 window.
- Other Macs. Only one M1 has been measured. M2, M3 and M4 should be faster, but no number is claimed.
- Campaign. Every mission loads and chains; not every one has been played end to end.
- Zombies. Grief and Turned need a second player, and there is no co-op yet.
- macOS audio. When the system's coreaudiod is unhealthy the campaign stalls on its first video. Check that afplay -t 1 /System/Library/Sounds/Tink.aiff takes about 1 s; restarting the Mac fixes it.
You need an Apple silicon Mac, macOS 14 or later, at least 20 GB free (the conversion peaks at about 10 GB and about 4 GB stays), Homebrew, and Steam for Mac signed in to the account that owns the game.
git clone https://github.com/adrbn/bo2-mac.git && cd bo2-mac
brew install llvm@17 cmake ninja libvpx unicorn
pip3 install capstone
scripts/make_app.sh --from-source
Open Black Ops II.app, point it at your game folder and let it convert: about 1 hour 45 on an M1, the campaign first in about 45 minutes. The campaign is
playable as soon as it is converted: play it then, and Zombies and multiplayer are converted when you first pick them
in the game's menu. Otherwise the conversion goes on through all three. If the disk falls under
8 GB free, the conversion stops cleanly and resumes where it was.
Updating, or if the conversion stops. Run git pull && scripts/make_app.sh --from-source in the repository
folder: what is already converted is kept and the conversion resumes. An update redoes only what its changes touch: a
fix to the runtime relinks the three modes in about 3 minutes on an M1 instead of converting again. If it still fails,
open an issue with the log it names.
The converter only accepts the exact Steam build, checked by SHA-256. The Steam executables are encrypted by Valve's
SteamStub wrapper and this repository provides no way to remove it: the converter expects the three decrypted
images in ~/.bo2-native/steam/ (t6sp.exe.unpacked.exe, t6mp.exe.unpacked.exe, t6zm.exe.unpacked.exe). You make
them yourself from the copy you bought, with a separate tool of your choice. Only the wrapper must go: the file names
above and the SHA-256 check tell you at once whether a file is right. Never share these files.
DLC. The launcher asks your Steam client which DLC your account owns, exactly as the game does on Windows. A DLC map plays when you own it and its files are in your game folder.
- This beta: the three modes from a fresh Steam copy, on other Macs than the one that built them. Your reports (Mac model, frame rate, what broke) decide what comes next. First outside report, 2026-11-05: on an M2 Pro (16 GB), the conversion completed and the game started, after three fixes found on the way (#4, #5, #6).
- No Terminal: one app to download and open, then drop the game folder on its window. It carries its tools already built, so nothing is compiled on your Mac but the game itself (macOS 26 or later; macOS 14 and 15 keep the Terminal install).
- Fully translated: the 46 code blocks that still run through the Unicorn interpreter are translated ahead of time, and every translated instruction is checked against the interpreter; any translated function can be sent back to the interpreter, to find a wrong one by halving.
- No shader wait: shaders built before the first match, instead of at launch (about 3 minutes in multiplayer) and during play (freezes when a new effect appears). Started: shaders now compile in batches, and the ones from the last sessions compile in the background at launch. In multiplayer on an M1 without Xcode (a few tries, not a benchmark), shader compiling during the first two minutes of a match went from 18–25 s to 10–14 s on a first launch and about 5 s on the next one; freezes over 300 ms went from 15–22 to 13–15, then 7. The first launch still freezes about as often.
- Shorter conversion: down from about 2.5 hours to 1 hour 45 on an M1 (2026-11-06, measured on all three modes: the preparation reads the executable once, the lift and the fold use every core the memory allows). An update now redoes only what changed (a runtime fix: about 3 minutes). Next: less optimisation for code that rarely runs. The three modes share only 4 % of their functions, so converting shared code once would gain little.
- Faster, without heat: the campaign is bound by the scheduler thread, not by rendering; multiplayer with 11 bots is bound by the server thread. Native rewrites of the hottest functions come next, then frame rates above 60 for 120 Hz screens.
- Controllers: vibration and aim assist.
- Together: real UDP sockets for Zombies co-op, Grief and Turned, and multiplayer over LAN. Then local split screen, which the PC version never had: two copies of the game drawn in one window, one controller each, joined over that LAN.
- Later: MetalFX, post-processing when the frame is presented, and replacement textures loaded from the player's own copy.
For a copy the user owns, on hardware the user owns.
- No engine source and no leaked code are used.
- Neither the input binary nor the recompiled output is distributed. No game file is included: the player needs their own Steam copy of Call of Duty: Black Ops II. The converter only accepts the exact Steam build (SHA-256), and ownership is checked each time the game starts by the player's own Steam client: the game refuses to run when Steam is not signed in or the account does not own it.
- The copy protection is executed as the game wrote it; nothing in it is patched out. This repository provides no way to remove Valve's SteamStub wrapper.

articles.title: Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave
articles.body:
I’ve been paranoid about my SSH keys for a while now. They just sit there in ~/.ssh/, protected by nothing but file permissions. Any malicious script that gets access to my filesystem could just copy them and get into all my servers.
Also, there have been many stories out there online about fake interview assignments that asked to clone a repo and run it on your local machine.
This is one of the reasons I switched completely to using devcontainers, but even that was not really enough for me (and it shouldn’t be enough for you or anybody else really).
So I finally decided to do something about it.
TL;DR
I have decided to NOT go with the native macOS Secure Enclave approach (using only out-of-the-box tools) because it ended up plain ugly and I can’t live with that. However, it is a fully functional, working solution that I would definitely use otherwise.
The Options
After some research, I found several ways to protect SSH keys:
- Native macOS Secure Enclave — no third-party apps, built into the OS
- Secretive — third-party app that stores keys in Secure Enclave
- YubiKey — hardware security key with FIDO2 support
- 1Password / Bitwarden — store keys in an encrypted vault, use their SSH agent
I already use 1Password, but I might switch to something else in the future. Bitwarden recently added SSH key support (even on the free tier!), but it’s still a software solution — the keys are encrypted at rest but decrypted in memory when used.
What I really wanted was hardware-backed security. The private key should literally be impossible to extract, even if my Mac is fully compromised.
That left me with YubiKey or Secure Enclave. I have a YubiKey 5C, but I wanted to try the native approach first — no extra hardware to carry around, no third-party apps to maintain.
What is Secure Enclave SSH?
Since macOS Sequoia (and Tahoe), macOS supports SSH keys backed by the Secure Enclave, a security subsystem on the Mac’s chip that is isolated from the main processor. The private key is created inside it and never leaves.
When you SSH somewhere, your Mac asks the Secure Enclave to sign the authentication challenge. If you enable Touch ID, you have to approve each signing operation. The actual private key never exists in memory or on disk.
The workflow is surprisingly similar to regular SSH keys:
Setting It Up
Step 1: Create the Secure Enclave Key
macOS provides the sc_auth command (Smart Card Authentication) to manage CryptoTokenKit identities. Despite the name, it works with Secure Enclave too.
sc_auth create-ctk-identity -l "ssh-MacBook" -k p-256-ne -t bio
Breaking this down:
- -l "ssh-MacBook" — a label for your reference (only visible locally)
- -k p-256-ne — NIST P-256 curve, non-exportable (the key can never leave Secure Enclave)
- -t bio — require biometric (Touch ID) for every use
You’ll be prompted for Touch ID to create the key.
Problem 1: Touch ID Error
When I first ran this command, I got a scary error:
Error: Error Domain=NSOSStatusErrorDomain Code=-25293 "Failed to generate keypair"
(errKCAuthFailed / errSecAuthFailed: / Authorization/Authentication failed.)
UserInfo={..., NSUnderlyingError=... "Failed to get bio catacomb UUID for user 502." ...}
Turns out my Touch ID enrollment got reset somehow. After re-enrolling my fingerprint in System Settings → Touch ID & Password, the command worked fine.
You can verify the key was created:
sc_auth list-ctk-identities
Output:
Key Type Public Key Hash                          Prot Label       Common Name  Valid To          Valid
p-256-ne A71277F0BC5825A7B3576D014F31282A866EF3BC bio  ssh-MacBook ssh-MacBook  2027-01-26, 10:18 YES
Step 2: Export the Key Handle
Now we need to create a “key handle” file that SSH can use. This is NOT the private key — it’s just a reference that tells SSH “go ask the Secure Enclave to sign this.”
ssh-keygen -w /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib -K -N ""
When prompted for PIN, just press Enter (it’s not used for biometric keys). Touch ID will pop up. This creates id_ecdsa_sk_rk and id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub in your current directory.
Move them to your SSH directory:
mv id_ecdsa_sk_rk* ~/.ssh/
Step 3: Configure SSH to Use the Secure Enclave Provider
Add this to your ~/.zshrc (or ~/.bashrc):
export SSH_SK_PROVIDER=/usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib
Reload your shell:
source ~/.zshrc
Problem 2: Outdated Commands Everywhere
If you search for “macOS Secure Enclave SSH” online, you’ll find a lot of guides telling you to run ssh-add -K. Don’t. It’s deprecated:
WARNING: The -K and -A flags are deprecated and have been replaced
         by the --apple-use-keychain and --apple-load-keychain
         flags, respectively.
And even the new flags don’t work for Secure Enclave keys — they’re for the traditional macOS Keychain, not CryptoTokenKit. The SSH_SK_PROVIDER environment variable is the correct approach.
Step 4: Get Your Public Key
cat ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub
Output:
sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... ssh:
That ssh: at the end is the FIDO2 application ID — it’s part of the key, not a comment. You can add your own comment after it when copying to authorized_keys:
sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... ssh: macbook-secure-enclave
Step 5: Copy to Your Server
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub user@your-server
Or manually paste the public key (with your comment) into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server.
Step 6: Configure ~/.ssh/config
Problem 3: SSH Doesn’t Find the Key
After setting everything up, I tried to SSH… and it asked for my password.
The verbose output (ssh -vvv) showed SSH was only trying my old RSA key:
debug1: Offering public key: /Users/sergii/.ssh/id_rsa RSA SHA256:...
The problem: SSH doesn’t automatically look for files named id_ecdsa_sk_rk. It only auto-discovers standard names like id_rsa, id_ed25519, id_ecdsa.
The fix is to explicitly add it to your ~/.ssh/config:
Host *
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
SSH tries identity files in order, so put the Secure Enclave key first if you want it to be the default.
⚠️ Note: If you’re using 1Password’s SSH agent (IdentityAgent), it might conflict with this setup. I had to comment it out while testing.
Step 7: Test It
ssh user@your-server
You should get a Touch ID prompt, then connect.
The Ugly Touch ID Prompt
One thing I’m not thrilled about: the Touch ID dialog says “ctccardtoken needs to authenticate to continue” instead of something friendly like “SSH wants to use your key.”
This is because the prompt comes from CryptoTokenKit — a low-level framework that Apple hasn’t polished for end-user SSH. If this bothers you, Secretive provides a much nicer UI while still using Secure Enclave under the hood.
Why Touch ID for Everything?
I initially thought about creating two keys — one with Touch ID for “important” servers, one without for convenience (like Git operations).
But then I realized: without -t bio, malware could use my key silently. With -t bio, I always know when something is using my SSH key. A few extra taps per day is a small price for that visibility.
So my recommendation if you’re planning to store your SSH keys this way: just use -t bio for everything. If it ever gets annoying, you can always create a second key later.
The Catch: No Backups
Secure Enclave keys are tied to your specific Mac. If your Mac dies, the keys die with it.
That’s by design: the key can’t be exported, so it can’t be backed up either. Keep more than one key instead. Add your Secure Enclave key AND a backup key (from a YubiKey, or another Mac) to your servers’ authorized_keys. If one device is lost, you still have access via the other.
Final Thoughts
It seems to be a proper way to store your SSH keys securely, and it is way better than storing them on your hard drive.
With the implementation above you get:
- ✅ Private key literally cannot be stolen (it’s in hardware)
- ✅ Every SSH operation requires Touch ID (I know when my key is used)
- ✅ No third-party apps needed
- ✅ Works with existing authorized_keys workflow
However, I’ve been somewhat surprised by the ugliness of the UI. Not sure why Apple released such an unpolished thing. In each and every presentation they have a section on security (where their Apple logo becomes an Apple lock), so I was expecting an actual aesthetically appealing look for their security features. It is definitely not the case. My sense of beauty is not compatible with this ugliness, so I will be looking into other solutions to store my SSH keys in Secure Enclave such as Secretive.
I also still need a backup option in case anything happens to my Mac.

articles.title: The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026
articles.body:
Find answers and ask new questions
Find answers
Use the search bar at the top of this page to quickly ask questions and find answers.
How to search the community
 
The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.
You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site.
We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.
Find answers. Ask questions. Connect with Apple customers around the world.
Get insights from experienced community members.
Once you sign in, tap your name at the top of the page. Tap View More and then Manage Subscriptions. There you can adjust the people and discussions you’re following.
How to manage subscriptions
As you participate in discussions, you earn points which can get you perks and more. You can even earn product specialties if you focus on specific product areas.

articles.title: Hooked on Tuna
articles.body:
From a humble mayonnaise-laden sandwich to an expensive piece of sashimi, tuna is a prized source of food for people around the world. Once an inexpensive, easily shipped canned protein source, today’s bluefin tunas can fetch millions of dollars at auction. Millions of tons of tuna are harvested every year, supporting a global industry worth around US$40 billion annually.
But tunas are more than just the pink flesh found in cans and sushi, and humanity’s story with these fish goes back further than you might expect.
As a biologist and an archaeologist interested in long-term human-environment interactions, we wanted to investigate the deep record of people’s relationship with tunas.
We drew on the expertise of 18 leading researchers worldwide and studied a variety of sources, from the skeletal remains of tunas in archaeological sites to ancient rock art, paintings on frescos and vases, written historical records and ethnographic accounts from Indigenous communities. This data helped us understand where, when and why people caught tunas, and what cultural and environmental forces shaped these early fisheries. In turn, this provided new insights into how past harvests compare with the millions of tons caught today.
An apex predator of the ocean
“Tuna” is a common name given to a group of 15 fish species. The major market species include eight “true tunas” in genus Thunnus along with skipjack tuna (Katsuwonus pelamis).
Tunas are among the largest predators in the open ocean, with some species reaching almost 10 feet (over 3 meters) in length and living for over 40 years. Tuna are champion swimmers; Pacific bluefin tuna can migrate 5,000 miles (8,000 kilometers) across the northern Pacific in a matter of months.
Tuna are also ecologically important apex predators and serve as sentinels of ocean health. However, most scientific research has focused on the past 75 years, with assessments of the health of tuna populations benchmarked against the year 1950. The focus on recent decades raises a variety of questions about the deeper history of fishing for tuna prior to the past century.
A deep and dynamic history
The oldest definitive evidence of tuna fishing, in the form of skeletal remains of what were likely skipjack tuna, comes from East Timor in southeast Asia about 44,000 years ago. Likely aided by deepwater channels that brought tunas close to shore, this early example of tuna fishing is somewhat unusual – most areas of the world don’t contain evidence of tuna fishing until 10,000 years ago or more recently.
Ancient fishers in Japan and Korea, for instance, captured tunas beginning at least 7,000 years ago, with a rich culinary tradition and large-scale harvests that trace their way to the present day love for these fishes in the region.
The northeastern Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea are home to one of the world’s oldest and most important tuna fisheries, focused on Atlantic bluefin tuna. A few ancient tuna bones found in a Neanderthal site in Gibraltar dating to around 26,000 years ago may have been obtained by Neanderthals scavenging. However, by 9,000 to 11,000 years ago, thousands of tuna bones were deposited in Greece in a cave overlooking Kiladha Bay. The number of sites across Europe with tuna remains increases rapidly in the archaeological record after about 8,000 years ago.
These early fishers used a variety of methods to catch tuna, including hook and line, harpoons, and traps or nets. They often took advantage of topographic features where fish could be driven close to shore. This tuna fishing is captured in written records, paintings and other art, showing the cultural importance of these fish to ancient European societies. The ancient Greeks deemed tuna worthy of sacrifice to the gods and used them as offerings to Poseidon.
By 3,000 years ago, a commercial Atlantic bluefin tuna fishery had formed in the Mediterranean, with large-scale trade and specialized nets and traps. By the 16th and 17th centuries, people may have caught tens of thousands of tons annually. This fishery was made possible by the predictable migration patterns of Atlantic bluefin and coastal access to tunas – no dangerous oceanic voyages necessary.
For over 5,000 years, Indigenous people on North America’s northwest coast, particularly in Nuu-chah-nulth territory, had an important and complex fishery for Pacific bluefin tuna.
Ethnographic accounts from native elders describe how during unique warm-water events in late summer, people voyaged out at night into the fjords, aided by natural bioluminescent plankton. With spotters overlooking the fjords and communicating from land, fishers set fires in canoes to lure tuna close enough to harpoon. People would spear these massive fish, some perhaps more than 6 feet (2 meters) in length and weighing 640 pounds (290 kilograms). Bluefin tuna vertebrae have been found in 23 regional archaeological sites.
In Southern California, people also captured tunas, particularly around Santa Catalina Island, where Indigenous fishers caught Pacific bluefin, yellowfin, albacore and skipjack tunas for 6,000 years, leaving the fishes’ skeletal remains in regional archaeological sites.
However, it wasn’t until the 19th and 20th centuries that commercial and sport fisheries for tuna developed in the area. Tuna experienced a meteoric rise in popularity during World War I and World War II. Often centered around canneries in Los Angeles and San Diego, Southern California commercial and industrial tuna fisheries benefited from Japanese and Portuguese immigrant fishing communities, which helped spawn a global industry for tuna.
Emergence of oceanic exploitation
Tuna consumption by people is obviously nothing new. But how has the scale of tuna harvest changed through time?
Using the quantity of tuna bones present in archaeological sites as a rough metric, we found that even the largest of these ancient fisheries – those in the Mediterranean – likely only removed thousands of tonnes of tuna over millennia, which pales in comparison to the millions of tons of tuna now removed from the oceans every year.
This contrast brings up important questions: What are the consequences of oceanic exploitation exploding over such a relatively short period of time? How can people sustainably manage tuna populations? There are no easy answers, and three of the commercially important tuna species – southern bluefin, Pacific bluefin and bigeye tuna – remain endangered, vulnerable or near threatened. However, in several regions a combination of effective governance, monitoring and harvest controls have stabilized tuna populations even with intensive harvests.
The deep history of tuna fishing also highlights the human capacity for innovation. For more than 44,000 years, people have found ways to locate, catch and share tunas. That same capacity, channeled into international cooperation and science-based management, may help maintain global tuna stocks at sustainable levels – even if they’ll likely never again reach precommercial fishing levels of abundance.

articles.title: Streaming is still trying to be TikTok
articles.body:
At Skydance’s first employee town hall after it acquired Warner Bros. Discovery in October, CEO David Ellison told staff that the company behind Paramount Plus and HBO Max was competing for people’s attention with some of the world’s biggest tech companies. Months earlier, he’d singled out a way to get viewers to spend more time with Paramount’s programming. A feed of short vertical videos, he said, was “critical to our future.”
Streaming is still trying to be TikTok
It hasn’t proven that short-form video will help.
It hasn’t proven that short-form video will help.
On Skydance’s earnings call Monday, Ellison put a name to the competition. Add up all of Paramount’s and Warner Bros. Discovery’s broadcast, cable, and streaming properties, he said, and they still trail YouTube in US television watch time, according to Nielsen. Ellison said Paramount Plus engagement had risen more than 20 percent since Skydance acquired Paramount last year. He didn’t mention how the clips feed panned out.
Over the past year, Disney Plus, Paramount Plus, Netflix, and HBO Max have introduced swipeable feeds of short videos in their mobile apps. A great scene can help a subscriber pick a show. A steady stream of clips could also get them to open the app when they only have a minute to spare. The bet is that both will make the subscription feel more worth paying for. But so far, the streamers have shared little about whether these feeds have succeeded in giving people another reason to stay subscribed.
On YouTube, a few clips can be the whole visit. YouTube accounted for a record 15.8 percent of viewing through US TV sets in August, according to Nielsen. YouTube also leads in time spent watching video on phones, where it competes with TikTok and Instagram, says Ross Benes, a senior analyst at eMarketer. The firm estimates that US adults spend a little over an hour and a half a day watching video on mobile devices and about two and a half hours on connected TVs. It counts simultaneous phone and TV viewing in both totals.
The streamers have plenty of shows to clip, but they’re up against social apps with millions of people making something new reacting to that existing content every day. A scene in a streaming app is a pitch for the full episode. On TikTok or YouTube, a creator’s reaction to that same episode can be the reason you open the app in the first place. There’s something to come back for, even when the show is between seasons.
About 43 percent of Disney Plus mobile users had interacted with Verts by October, Disney said. The feed launched in March and lets viewers swipe through scenes, save titles, or jump straight into a movie or show. Disney didn’t say whether Verts gets people to watch more movies and shows or stay subscribed longer. Verts accounted for 65 percent of user-initiated short-form video starts in the ESPN app. A highlight from last night’s game gives fans something to watch even if they have no plans to sit through a full game.
On Disney Plus, the company is turning to fan-made videos in a more direct bid to compete with social video. In August, Disney announced a US pilot with TikTok to bring clips about its movies and shows into Verts. The feed will feature a curated selection from creators who opt in, and the clips will appear on both apps. On Disney’s August earnings call, CEO Josh D’Amaro said the deal could make Disney Plus a “stickier app” where people stay longer and discover more, which “benefits our whole ecosystem.” An internal roadmap reviewed by Business Insider targets early 2027 for adding creator content and calls for sports and news clips and short-form series such as microdramas.
Disney has shown that people will use a clips feed inside a streaming app. The next question is whether the feed becomes a reason to open the app in the first place, and another reason to keep paying for it.
Paramount is looking beyond its own catalog, too. After adding a clips feed to Paramount Plus in April, it was exploring user-generated video for a possible free tier by September. On Paramount’s May earnings call, Ellison said viewers were going from clips to news, sports, and entertainment, without saying how often.
HBO Max began testing Shorts with select US iPhone users in July, letting viewers jump straight from a clip into a movie or show. Skydance’s third-quarter results excluded HBO Max because the quarter ended six days before the Warner Bros. Discovery deal closed. The company gave no usage figures for either feed on its November call.
At Netflix, Jefferies estimates that average monthly viewing fell from 66 hours per member in the first half of 2023 to 49 in the first half of 2026. On Netflix’s October earnings call, co-CEO Greg Peters pointed to lower cancellation rates in the US and globally as evidence that engagement remained healthy.
On the same call, co-CEO Ted Sarandos downplayed the role of short-form video six months after Netflix made Clips a centerpiece of its mobile redesign. He grouped short-form video with other early experiments and said Netflix’s core entertainment business still accounted for roughly 95 percent of spending and nearly all revenue. Netflix plans to roll out themed Clips feeds in 2027, but it hasn’t said whether Clips gets people to watch more.
Making money from the feed itself is harder. Benes says ads on phones generally fetch less than ads on TVs, and a short clip has less room for ad breaks than a movie or an episode. “I just don’t see it being like a big success for them,” he says. He sees a more plausible role for these feeds as something to scroll through on your phone while the TV is on.
Streamers may end up borrowing something useful from TikTok: a better way to browse. Their business still depends on what people settle in to watch.

articles.title: Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890)
articles.body:
Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890)
Approved July 2, 1890, The Sherman Anti-Trust Act was the first Federal act that outlawed monopolistic business practices.
The Sherman Anti-trust Act of 1890 was the first measure passed by the U.S. Congress to prohibit trusts. It was named for Senator John Sherman of Ohio, who was a chairman of the Senate finance committee and the Secretary of the Treasury under President Hayes.
Several states had passed similar laws, but they were limited to intrastate businesses. The Sherman Antitrust Act was based on the constitutional power of Congress to regulate interstate commerce. (For more background, see previous milestone documents: the Constitution, Gibbons v. Ogden, and the Interstate Commerce Act.)
The Sherman Anti-Trust Act passed the Senate by a vote of 51–1 on April 8, 1890, and the House by a unanimous vote of 242–0 on June 20, 1890. President Benjamin Harrison signed the bill into law on July 2, 1890.
A trust is an arrangement by which stockholders in several companies transfer their shares to a single set of trustees. In exchange, the stockholders receive a certificate entitling them to a specified share of the consolidated earnings of the jointly managed companies.
Toward the end of the 19th century, trusts come to dominate a number of major industries, destroying competition. For example, on January 2, 1882, the Standard Oil Trust was formed. Attorney Samuel Dodd of Standard Oil first had the idea of a trust. A board of trustees was set up, and all the Standard properties were placed in its hands. Every stockholder received 20 trust certificates for each share of Standard Oil stock. All the profits of the component companies were sent to the nine trustees, who determined the dividends. The nine trustees elected the directors and officers of all the component companies. This allowed Standard Oil to function as a monopoly since the nine trustees ran all the component companies.
The Sherman Anti-Trust Act authorized the federal government to institute proceedings against trusts in order to dissolve them. Any combination "in the form of trust or otherwise that was in restraint of trade or commerce among the several states, or with foreign nations" was declared illegal. Persons forming such combinations were subject to fines of $5,000 and a year in jail. Individuals and companies suffering losses because of trusts were permitted to sue in federal court for triple damages.
The act was designed to restore competition, but it was loosely worded and failed to define such critical terms as "trust," "combination," "conspiracy," and "monopoly." Five years later, the Supreme Court dismantled the act in United States v. E. C. Knight Company (1895). The Court ruled that the American Sugar Refining Company, one of the defendants in the case, had not violated the law even though the company controlled about 98% of all sugar refining in the United States. The Supreme Court reasoned that the company’s control of manufacture did not constitute a control of trade.
The E. C. Knight ruling seemed to end any government regulation of trusts. In spite of this, during President Theodore Roosevelt’s "trust busting" campaigns at the turn of the century, the Sherman Anti-Trust Act was used with considerable success. In 1904, the Supreme Court upheld the government’s suit to dissolve the Northern Securities Company in Northern Securities Co. v. United States. By 1911, President Taft had used the act against the Standard Oil Company and the American Tobacco Company. In the late 1990s, in another effort to ensure a competitive free market system, the federal government used the Sherman Anti-Trust Act, then over 100 years old, against the giant Microsoft computer software company.

Every stretch of Interstate, U.S. highway and designated EV corridor in the 50 states and DC longer than 50 miles with no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line, and beside it the federal compliance figure: stretches with no fast charger within 1 mile of the highway (the federal NEVI siting distance). From our daily check of every open public fast charger.
Quick answer · November 11, 2026
How many U.S. highway stretches run 50 miles with no fast charger within 5 miles?
According to ChargingNear.me, as of November 11, 2026, 852 U.S. highway stretches run over 50 miles with no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway (straight-line). The longest is 455.5 miles of US-160 in Kansas. 961 stretches have no fast charger within 1 mile of the highway (the federal NEVI siting distance).
The headline is the practical measure, the one that matters to a driver: no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line. The federal NEVI program sites funded chargers within 1 mile of a corridor, so the compliance figure beside it uses no fast charger within 1 mile of the highway (the federal NEVI siting distance).

How many stretches over 50 miles each state has under each measure and the miles they cover, as of November 11, 2026. A state shows 0 when we found no stretch over 50 miles without open public DC fast chargers (any network, any plug) listed by the U.S. Department of Energy, within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line (the practical columns) or open public DC fast chargers (any network, any plug) listed by the U.S. Department of Energy, within 1 mile of the highway (the federal NEVI siting distance), measured in a straight line (the 1-mile columns), on any Interstate, U.S. highway or designated EV corridor in it. Under the 5-mile measure, 8 show 0: Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Vermont.
Highway gaps over 50 miles in each state and DC under both measures, as of November 11, 2026
The National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program pays states to build fast chargers along designated Alternative Fuel Corridors. Its rule, 23 CFR 680.106, sets the minimum for a funded station: at least four CCS ports, each able to deliver 150 kilowatts at the same time. Federal guidance from February 2022 treated a state’s Interstates as fully built out once such chargers stood every 50 miles, within 1 travel mile of the Interstate. The interim final guidance of August 11, 2025 superseded it and leaves spacing to each state.
This page uses the 50-mile mark for every state so the numbers compare, and counts any open public DC fast charger, of any network and any plug, Tesla Superchargers included. The 1-mile figure follows the federal siting distance; the 5-mile figure counts chargers a driver can reach with a short detour. Of the 15,933 fast stations we checked, 2,592 meet every NEVI minimum; the rest still count as chargers here.
How to read the tables
Practical gap
A stretch of highway longer than 50 miles with no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line: between two such chargers in a row, or between one and a state line, the Canada or Mexico border, or the end of the highway. Any open public DC fast charger counts, on any network and with any plug.
1-mile NEVI gap
The same, with no fast charger within 1 mile of the highway (the federal NEVI siting distance). Every practical gap lies inside one of these; a 1-mile gap can hold none, one or several practical gaps.
Highway
As signed, such as I-70 or US-2. Other designated corridors keep the Federal Highway Administration’s name. In Colorado the highway links to our corridor guide for that road.
State
Where the stretch is. A highway that crosses a state line is split there, so one long empty road can appear as two gaps.
Miles
Distance along the highway between the two ends, to one decimal.
From and To
What starts and ends the gap. A charger is placed at the point on the highway nearest it. A charger with a page on ChargingNear.me is named and linked; a charger without one shows as a fast charger in its town. State lines, borders and highway ends are named as they are.
Chargers 1–5 mi off
Each open public DC fast charger more than 1 and at most 5 miles, in a straight line, from the nearest point of a 1-mile gap, its ends included: name, town, network, fast ports, plugs, miles off the highway and the highway mile nearest it. Exits are not in our data, so the exit you take may be a mile or two from that mile.
Data
Report a data error: tell us what is wrong with that row. A person on our team checks every report.
Methodology
Highway lines and mile markers come from FHWA’s Highway Performance Monitoring System (HPMS, 2024 data year): every mainline section a state signed as Interstate or U.S. highway. Several states leave that signing blank in HPMS (Texas, California, Maryland and Delaware among them), so a section’s signing also comes from FHWA’s National Highway System dataset, which records the posted route for the same HPMS route IDs. A number is kept in a state only when the state’s list of Interstate and U.S. highways has it (Wikipedia’s “List of Interstate Highways in” and “List of U.S. Highways in” each state, retrieved November 11, 2026), so a state highway never appears under an Interstate or U.S. number. Sections of one highway in one state are joined end to end; a second carriageway or couplet drawn beside the first is dropped. Where a highway runs on another highway’s road and the state files that road under the other number, its line follows that road between its own pieces (shared_road_miles, shared_with), unless the highway has a road of its own beside it there or the join would make it longer in the state than its route list says. Roads FHWA designates that are not Interstate or U.S. highways (state routes, parkways, turnpikes) use FHWA’s own corridor lines.
Mile markers come from the route measure each state reports to FHWA in HPMS, where it runs continuously along the line (state_route_measure). It often matches the posted mileposts (it does for I-70 in Colorado) but not always: some states measure from a different starting point or by section. Where the measure does not run continuously, such as one that restarts by county, the markers are miles from the south or west end of the line within the state (from_south_or_west_end).
Chargers are AFDC stations listed as open and public with at least one DC fast port, any network and any plug, including Tesla. In this file a charger serves a highway when it is within 5 miles of it in a straight line, so each row is a stretch with no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line. A driver can reach those chargers with a short detour, such as the Kalispell, Montana chargers 2 to 4 miles from US-2. Chargers just across a state line count.
We walk each highway from end to end and record every stretch longer than 50 miles between consecutive chargers, or between a charger and a state line, the Canada or Mexico border, or the end of the highway. A charger is placed at the point on the highway nearest it. Gap length is measured along the highway.
A charger sits at the same point on the highway under both measures, so every practical gap lies inside one 1-mile NEVI gap (nevi_gap_id); a 1-mile gap can hold none, one or several practical gaps.
Why 50 miles: FHWA’s February 10, 2022 NEVI guidance treated a state’s corridors as fully built out when chargers were installed every 50 miles along its Interstates, within 1 travel mile of the Interstate. FHWA’s August 11, 2025 interim final guidance superseded it and leaves spacing to each state. 23 CFR part 680 itself sets no spacing. We use 50 miles everywhere so states can be compared.
Corridor designation comes from FHWA’s Alternative Fuel Corridors map (Round 8), matched to the highway lines within 0.1 mile. A corridor named for another road counts only where that road has no line of its own there.
Before a new day’s gap files publish, automatic checks test them against the station database: no charger may sit within the measure’s distance of a gap over 100 miles, no practical gap may pass within 5 miles of a town where the database lists a DC fast charger, ends, mile markers and lengths must agree, every state’s highways must have been walked, counts and miles may not swing more than 10% from the day before, and fixed spot checks must pass, among them US-2 through Kalispell, Montana and US-82 through Artesia, New Mexico. If any check fails, the previous day’s files stay up.
Chargers are AFDC stations listed as open and public with at least one DC fast port, any network and any plug, including Tesla. In this file a charger serves a highway when it is within 1 mile of it in a straight line, the siting distance in FHWA’s 2022 NEVI guidance, so each row is a stretch with no fast charger within 1 mile of the highway (the federal NEVI siting distance). Chargers just across a state line count.
Chargers 1 to 5 miles off: every charger more than 1 and at most 5 miles, in a straight line, from the nearest point of the stretch, its ends included, so a charger in a town at either end is listed too. The mile marker given is the stretch’s point nearest the charger; exits are not in our data, so the exit a driver takes may be a mile or two from it.
The gap files are rebuilt every day from our copy of the Alternative Fuels Data Center list; this page reads the latest build, made November 11, 2026. Read the full open data methodology.
Straight-line distance from the charger to the highway, not driving distance to the exit; driving distance is not in our data.
Where two highways share a road, each highway’s line runs along it, so those miles appear under both. Where FHWA’s data cannot confirm the shared road, the highway’s line stops at the junction and starts again after it, and its gaps end there (highway_end).
Where a state’s road file leaves a U.S. highway unsigned for a stretch, the line follows the road between its two pieces when that road is in the same file, ends at each piece point at the other, and the road runs at most 1.5 times the straight line plus a mile, up to 15 miles apart. Elsewhere the line breaks, and a gap ending there is described as ending “where FHWA’s line for it breaks”: the highway goes on, so the gap may be longer. Some states sign few U.S. highways in the file at all (Alabama files most of its U.S. mileage under state route numbers), so their highways have more breaks.
Chargers in Canada and Mexico are not in AFDC’s U.S. listing, so a gap ending at a border may be shorter in practice.
A charger listed as open in AFDC may be down on a given day; the gaps assume it works.
How to drive across a long gap
Look a few miles off the highway first. The 1-mile table lists fast chargers 1 to 5 miles off each stretch. A short detour into a town can save a long, tense run.
Leave with a buffer. Charge higher than usual before the gap starts. Arriving at the far end with 15 to 20 percent left leaves room for a detour or a charger that is down.
Expect less range than the sticker. Cold, headwinds, climbs, rain and highway speed all shorten range; in deep winter a gap that looks easy on paper may not be.
Warm the battery first. Many cars precondition the battery when you navigate to a fast charger, so set the last one before the gap as your destination.
Know your backup. Hotels, campgrounds and town centers inside a gap often have Level 2 chargers: slow, but enough overnight. Each state page lists them by city.
Check both ends the day you drive. A station listed as open can be out of service. Station pages on ChargingNear.me show the latest driver check-ins when there are any. Our Will I Make It tool checks a trip against your car’s range.
Why the list changes
The lists are rebuilt every day, so they move as the network does. A gap shrinks or disappears when a new fast charger opens near the highway, and a new one can appear when a station closes or drops off the federal list. One new station in the middle of a long gap splits it into two shorter ones, and if both halves run under 50 miles, the gap leaves the table. Before a day’s files publish, automatic checks test them against our station database; if one fails, the previous day’s files stay up. Each version is numbered, and its changelog on our open data page records what changed.
Who uses these lists
The files are built for state transportation departments, metropolitan planning organizations, utilities, charging companies and journalists: to see where corridors still need investment, to check announced projects against what is actually open, and to report on progress. Each row carries coordinates and mile markers, so the gaps load straight into mapping software such as QGIS or ArcGIS. Quote a gap with its measure and its date; credit ChargingNear.me.
Download, reuse and cite
Practical gaps: no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line
Download CSVJSON852 rows, version 2, last changed November 11, 2026
1-mile NEVI gaps: no fast charger within 1 mile of the highway (the federal NEVI siting distance)
Download CSVJSON961 rows, version 13, last changed November 11, 2026
Fast chargers 1 to 5 miles off each 1-mile NEVI gap
Download CSVJSON2,956 rows, version 3, last changed November 11, 2026
The files add mile markers, coordinates and corridor designation for each gap; column dictionaries, methodology and the changelog are on our open data page. Copies on Hugging Face and Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23984554) predate the November 11, 2026 correction; use the files here for current figures.

Cite as: ChargingNear.me. “U.S. highway practical charging gaps over 50 miles with no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway.” US EV Charging Open Data, version 2, November 11, 2026. https://chargingnear.me/data#us-highway-practical-charging-gaps. CC BY 4.0.
As of November 11, 2026, the longest stretch of U.S. highway with no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line is 455.5 miles of US-160 in Kansas, from Colorado state line to Jay Hatfield Chevrolet Columbus. Next is 374.3 miles of US-212 in South Dakota. The longest stretch with no fast charger within 1 mile of the highway (the federal NEVI siting distance) is 455.5 miles of US-160 in Kansas.
Why does this page use two distances?
Drivers will detour a few miles for a charger, so the headline counts a charger within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line. Federal NEVI guidance sites funded chargers within 1 mile, so we show that figure beside it for agencies. On US-2 in Montana, chargers in Kalispell sit 2 to 4 miles off the highway: they count under the 5-mile measure and are listed by name under the 1-mile one.
What is a highway charging gap?
A stretch of Interstate, U.S. highway or designated EV corridor longer than 50 miles between open public DC fast chargers, or between one and a state line, border or highway end. A practical gap has no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line; a 1-mile NEVI gap has no fast charger within 1 mile of the highway (the federal NEVI siting distance). Any network and any plug count, Tesla included. We use 50 miles everywhere so states compare fairly.
Which state has the most EV charging gaps?
As of November 11, 2026, Texas has the most stretches over 50 miles with no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line: 92, covering 8,101 miles. 43 states have at least one. The state table on this page shows both measures and sorts by count or miles.
Are there EV charging gaps on Interstate highways?
Yes. As of November 11, 2026, 110 stretches of Interstate run over 50 miles with no fast charger within 5 miles of the highway, measured in a straight line. The longest is 137.2 miles of I-94 in Montana, from Tesla Supercharger to Tesla Supercharger. 129 Interstate stretches have no fast charger within 1 mile of the highway (the federal NEVI siting distance).
How many charging stations meet NEVI standards?
In our daily check of November 11, 2026, 2,592 of the 15,933 open public DC fast stations in the 50 states and DC meet all three federal NEVI minimums: at least four CCS ports, each able to deliver 150 kW at the same time, within one mile of a designated Alternative Fuel Corridor. Our EV charging stations by state page shows the count for every state.

articles.title: Google’s AlphaGenome 2 zooms in on the cellular roots of disease
articles.body:
Researchers at Google DeepMind have unveiled a new AI model designed to unravel how changes in our DNA affect different cells, giving scientists a more detailed view of a notoriously difficult problem that could hold important clues to the causes of disease — and point the way to new treatments.
Google’s AlphaGenome 2 zooms in on the cellular roots of disease
DeepMind’s new DNA model better predicts how mutations affect different cells, potentially opening paths to treatment.
AlphaGenome 2 is the successor to DeepMind’s genome-predicting AI model AlphaGenome, which was released last year. While nearly every cell in the human body carries the same DNA, different types of cells — from heart muscle cells and skin cells to immune cells fighting an infection — switch different genes on and off, and those patterns can change depending on what a cell is doing. As a result, the same genetic variant can have very different effects depending on the type and state of the cell.
The new model is designed to capture those differences, predicting the effects of genetic variants on individual cell types and states. Google said in a blog post published Wednesday that it offers a much finer-grained view than broader models like AlphaGenome, potentially revealing disease-relevant effects in specific cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.
AlphaGenome 2 was trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues to give it that more detailed view. DeepMind says the model effectively turns static cell atlases — huge data repositories that map and catalog individual cells in detail — “into a predictive engine for human genetics.” According to the company, AlphaGenome 2 identifies nearly twice as many variants that can change gene expression in cells than its previous state-of-the-art model.
Notably, the researchers found that AlphaGenome 2 could also make predictions about new types of cells and biological states without needing to be retrained. It could also identify gaps in experimental data, potentially helping scientists decide what to investigate next in the lab.
For Adam Gayoso, a research scientist at Google DeepMind involved in the project, the big breakthrough is “tying human genetics to cell biology.” AlphaGenome 2 gives researchers a way to drill down on genetic variants identified in large populations, to see what effects they may be having on a cellular level, and potentially connect those effects to disease, he told The Verge.
Google DeepMind’s genomics lead Žiga Avsec told The Verge that this specificity is important if you have a goal like figuring out how to treat a particular disease. “When you develop drugs, you’re targeting specific proteins and specific cell types,” he explained, which makes having this kind of granularity vital.
Building a model like AlphaGenome 2 has only recently become possible thanks to new technologies that can capture individual cells and their states at high resolution and create the vast datasets needed to train it, Avsec said. DeepMind is now working to improve its genetics models by generating more data, including for cell states that aren’t represented well today. Avsec said future versions could also potentially be trained on data “across multiple species,” giving the models a broader view of biology. Longer term, he said models like AlphaGenome 2 could feed into efforts to create “virtual cells,” digital simulations designed to mimic biological systems.
Although Avsec said he views AlphaGenome 2 as a successor to AlphaGenome, it isn’t replacing it any time soon. He said its more detailed predictions come at a computational cost and are “more expensive” to produce than those of its predecessor, he said. Those demands would have made it impractical to use AlphaGenome 2 to produce the genome-wide Atlas covering “every possible DNA letter change in the human genome” that DeepMind released in September.
Google says it is making AlphaGenome 2 available for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API from today, with a limited “private preview” for commercial research.
The model is the latest in a growing array of efforts by Google and rival AI labs to use the technology to tackle major problems in science and medicine. Pushmeet Kohli, who heads DeepMind’s AI for science research, has hinted that more impressive scientific results are on the way, and the organization is expected to open an automated materials science lab in the UK soon. Anthropic, meanwhile, has been experimenting with drug design and given Claude a wet lab, while OpenAI has been mowing down an impressive amount of longstanding problems in mathematics and related fields.

articles.title: Google Fi Brings Back Network Switching With 'Secondary' Partner
articles.body:
Google Fi Brings Back Network Switching With 'Secondary' Partner 15
			
		 	
				Google Fi is bringing back network switching through an unnamed "secondary" 5G carrier. "Most users will be on the 'Primary network,' but Google Fi will automatically switch users to the 'Secondary network' if it meaningfully improves performance with so-called 'smart thresholds' for doing so," reports 9to5Google. "At launch, there is no manual switching." When Project Fi first launched the service included support with both Sprint and T-Mobile. That went away when T-Mobile acquired Sprint in 2020. 9to5Google reports:  Google is not naming the second network today, but did share that Ultra Wideband is supported. Officially, you are switching between "two of America's fastest 5G networks."
Fi Wireless does note that users have top priority, so data is never deprioritized on the Primary network. Meanwhile, there's "highest QCI priority" on the backup network that means subscribers are among the last to be slowed down when there's congestion. This is also available internationally when local partner networks are available with the Flexible and Unlimited Premium plans.
Network switching will first be supported on Pixel 9 and newer devices that have a Google Fi eSIM (and no other SIM active). It makes use of Android's Multiple Enabled Profiles (MEP) eSIM technology that allows for two carrier profiles on a single chip. [...] These Google Fi updates start rolling out today, with network switching seeing gradual availability.

articles.title: Oura is acquiring medical AI chatbot startup Counsel Health
articles.body:
Oura announced its quarterly earnings today and said it agreed to acquire Counsel Health for $625 million, after adding the company’s AI chatbot to its app earlier this year. Counsel Health calls itself an “AI-native primary care company,” using the app to deliver AI-generated responses and insights based on users’ health data reported from their wearables that can then proceed to a conversation with one of its in-house physicians.
Oura is acquiring medical AI chatbot startup Counsel Health
Doctor visits could start with a readout of your Oura ring data.
Oura says it expects the deal to close before the end of the year.
Oura CEO Tom Hale said in an interview with Bloomberg that the acquisition is part of a plan to connect wearables, clinical AI, and access to doctors based on insights from biometric data to answer questions or monitor ongoing conditions. Counsel Health’s AI chatbot can connect Oura users to a real doctor directly from the app and draw on users’ biometric data from their wearables in its answers to medical questions. The plan they describe in the press release is to focus on three areas, including preventative care, acute care for episodic health concerns, and specialty and chronic care for things like reproductive and cardiometabolic health.
According to Bloomberg, Counsel Health’s CEO Muthu Alagappan says it’s also planning to expand its network of on-demand physicians, which is currently “made up of about 50 people.” Counsel’s 70 employees will join Oura as part of the deal, with Alagappan becoming Oura’s chief clinical AI officer. Oura says in its announcement that Counsel will also continue offering its medical AI platform outside of Oura’s user base through new and existing enterprise partners, including “health plans, health systems, consumer health organizations, and employers.”

articles.title: Blender 5.3 Released With Nvidia DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction, Vulkan Default
articles.body:
Blender 5.3 Released With Nvidia DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction, Vulkan Default (phoronix.com) 6
			
		 	
				Blender 5.3 has been released with support for 3D Gaussian Splats, Nvidia DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction and Vulkan as the default graphics backend on Linux. Phoronix reports:  Blender now allows importing Gaussian Splats from PLY, SPZ, and glTF files. Also new to Blender 5.3 is NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support as a new denoiser. Blender 5.3 also brings support for NVIDIA RTX Spark devices.
For the Cycles code in Blender 5.3 the Principled BSDF for shader nodes now supports dispersion. Another notable change with Blender 5.3 is the Vulkan back-end now being the default on Windows (except for Windows on ARM) and Linux systems. Vulkan 1.1 or newer is required and should deliver better performance than OpenGL.

articles.title: Apple is killing its Support Community forum next week
articles.body:
It’s the end of the road for the Apple Support Community. The dedicated discussion forum, which gave Apple users a place to exchange advice, troubleshoot, and generally chat about Apple products, has been placed into read-only mode, with a message from the company announcing that the Support Community will shut down for good on November 20th.
Apple is killing its Support Community forum next week
The Apple Support Community platform is now read-only, and will permanently close on November 20th.
Here’s the full banner notice that’s currently displayed on the website:
“The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site. We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.”
The Apple Support Community has undergone several name changes over the years, but its history as an online forum for providing user-to-user tech support goes back to 1998, when it first launched as the Apple Tech Exchange. Apple hasn’t specified what will happen to the decades worth of Support Community posts when the platform shuts down next week. Presumably, they’ll all disappear with it.
In a statement to MacRumors, Apple said it decided to sunset the Apple Support Community after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs. We have reached out to Apple for comment.

articles.title: Open research, stronger privacy: Making Firefox users harder to fingerprint
articles.body:
Firefox is strengthening protection against trackers that recognize you across websites, even when they don’t use cookies. The latest fingerprinting protections shipped in Firefox reduce the extractable distinguishing details, making more Firefox users look alike to tracking scripts and strengthening individuals’ privacy in everyday browsing.
These protections build on our research into browser and device fingerprinting, a technique that combines details about your browser and device to identify you across websites. We investigated which details contribute most to make users uniquely identifiable, turned those findings into practical protections for Firefox users, and shared our results openly so the wider web security and privacy community can build stronger defenses.
Our findings are documented in the research paper Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild, which has been accepted for publication at Computer and Communications Security (CCS) 2026, a leading international conference on computer security and privacy. We’ve also created an easier-to-digest website and browser test suite to help explore the findings in the paper.
Cookie-less Tracking
Browser fingerprinting combines details about your browser and device, such as available fonts, screen dimensions, and graphics hardware, to build a uniquely recognizable profile. Each piece may seem ordinary, but together, they can enable trackers to single you out across websites, even without storing a cookie.
Effective fingerprinting protection starts with understanding which browser details trackers rely on most. Our research found that protecting just a handful of browser features can significantly weaken popular fingerprinting techniques. That finding enabled us to focus on Firefox’s protections where they can make the biggest difference and bring those benefits to all Firefox users.
To evaluate these techniques, we simulated the browser measurements collected by fingerprinting scripts from Fingerprint Pro, Signifyd, and Akamai and examined how their combinations distinguish users. The study used measurements collected from nearly 25 million Firefox users, with additional privacy safeguards beyond Mozilla’s existing data collection policies.
Those safeguards included OHTTP, which routed encrypted requests through a relay. The relay sees the user’s IP address but not the request contents, while Mozilla receives the contents without the user’s IP address. We also tightly limited data access and retention: individual telemetry records were deleted several months ago and only aggregate results were retained and published for open science. Our research paper explains the method, safeguards and ethical considerations in detail.
Less distinctive, more private
Our approach reduces unnecessary differences in the information Firefox exposes to websites. For example, Firefox limits the information exposed through screen resolution APIs to hide the size and position of the system taskbar or dock, preventing that desktop layout detail from contributing to a fingerprint. As another example, it can report processor counts as either 4 or 8 instead of exposing the exact count, which can make a browser more distinctive.
Our goal is to make more users’ browsers look similar to fingerprinting scripts while preserving the information websites need to function correctly, like language and timezone settings. Firefox also uses randomization to make other fingerprinting signals less useful to trackers, though the benefits of these techniques are harder to quantify and fall outside the measurements reported here.
In our evaluation, these protections (the most recent of which shipped in Firefox 145) substantially degraded the precision of fingerprinting in Firefox both by reducing the number of users with unique fingerprints and increasing the size of the groups of users that share a fingerprint.
The research also enabled us to identify why certain measurements differed between users. Addressing these differences produced more consistent outputs for image rendering, Web Audio, and mathematical operations on Android, reducing the distinguishing details available to fingerprinters.
These results show that substantial reductions in browser fingerprint uniqueness are achievable and provide meaningful progress toward stronger online privacy. These do not make fingerprinting impossible as trackers can surely adapt. But our research provides a concrete, measurable improvement in browser defenses against online tracking.
The built-in privacy protections in Firefox are complemented with capabilities and options to further strengthen the protection against online fingerprinters. Built-in and always-on Total Cookie Protection in Firefox segments stateful identifiers and prevents trackers from following you across your browsing using cookies. Firefox Relay provides you with unique email masks, preventing websites from linking your subscriptions to other sites via data brokers. And Firefox now integrates a free VPN that masks your IP address to protect against tracking and fingerprinting. Together with Firefox’s enhanced fingerprinting protections, these capabilities provide everyone a very strong foundation to take back control of their privacy online.
Research that improves everyday browsing
Privacy protections need to work on the websites people use every day. These findings allow us to prioritize changes that deliver measurable privacy benefits while keeping those websites working.
Some of Firefox’s fingerprinting protections, such as hiding the size of your taskbar or dock, are on by default in all browsing modes. Others are introduced first in Private Browsing and Strict Enhanced Tracking Protection (ETP) mode, while we work toward enabling them by default, following the same strategy we’ve used for years. To enable these additional protections in all your Firefox windows, select Strict in the Enhanced Tracking Protection settings. Follow the steps here if the “Strict” protections get in the way of any website functionality.
Want to explore browser fingerprinting yourself? Visit the research project page to try the fingerprinting test and learn more about our findings. For a closer look at what we measured and how we turned those insights into Firefox protections, explore our paper: Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild.
We’ll keep strengthening Firefox’s privacy protections while continuing to work in the open. By sharing our research, our code, and what we learn, we’re shaping the web we envision: free, private, secure, and accessible to all.

articles.title: Six Math Essentials by Terence Tao
articles.body:
Terence Tao · original page
In Six Math Essentials, the renowned mathematician and Fields Medalist Terence Tao introduces readers to six central concepts that have guided mathematicians from antiquity to the frontiers of what we know today and now help us make sense of our complex world. This slim, elegant volume explores numbers as the gateway to quantitative thinking; algebra as the gateway to abstraction; geometry as a way to calculate beyond what we can see; probability as a tool to navigate uncertainty with rigorous thinking; analysis as a means to tame the very large or the very small; and dynamics as the mathematics of change.
No errata have been recorded for this book.

articles.title: Europe Must Rethink Security As Big Tech Power Grows, EU Says
articles.body:
Europe Must Rethink Security As Big Tech Power Grows, EU Says (reuters.com) 37
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Reuters: The European Union must rethink security to take into account challenges and risks posed by the growing power of major technology companies that go beyond traditional competition concerns, European Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera said on Monday. "We need to review and to deepen our concept of security, including cybersecurity," Ribera told reporters in Lisbon, arguing that testing and monitoring devices connected to critical infrastructure was no longer sufficient and that security means also ensuring that the Big Tech companies are "governed by democratic and transparent patterns." "We need to be quite quick in the deployment of these new approaches ... This is one of the most critical topics for security, for democracy, and for (our) values," she said.

articles.title: EventSourcingDB 1.3.0 Is Available
articles.body:
EventSourcingDB 1.3.0 is Available
EventSourcingDB 1.3.0 is out, and it is faster and more stable than any version before it. Writing and EventQL queries are considerably faster, reading is faster as well, every request is bounded in time, and more than sixty fixes went in. Next to all that, it brings a new API that reports the outcome of every request it accepts in its body and names every error with a code of its own.
This post walks through what changed and what to mind when you upgrade. The v1 API is supported until January 31, 2027, and a later release removes it, so you can move to the new one at your own pace. And from today on, the documentation of EventSourcingDB lives on eventfoundation.io; every old link leads there.
A New API, Built to Last#
The new v2 API runs next to the v1 API, on the same data. Its central idea is simple: once the server has accepted a request, its outcome is in the body. A request counts as accepted when it is authenticated, its body has the shape its route expects, and it stays within its limits. A precondition that does not hold, an event type that is not known, a database in read-only mode – all of these come back as an answer the client can read, rather than as a status code it has to interpret.
Every error carries a code that is a link to its own page, which explains why it happens and how to fix it. You will find them all under Errors. Streamed answers that come to an end, such as reading events, close with an explicit end item, so a client can tell a complete answer from one that was cut off. While a stream waits, the server sends heartbeats through it, which keeps a proxy from closing it in between.
The v2 API also brings recursive preconditions: isSubjectPristine, isSubjectPopulated, and isSubjectOnEventId can now apply to a subject together with every subject below it. That is useful whenever a decision depends on a whole part of the tree rather than a single subject.
The current versions of all eight client SDKs speak both APIs and use the v2 API wherever the server offers it. So apart from updating your SDK, you do not have to change your code, as long as a proxy in front of the database lets through the HTTP method QUERY, which the v2 API uses for reading. If you call the HTTP API directly, Migrating to v2 shows what changes, route by route.
Moving and Backing Up Data#
Exporting and importing make it easier to move events into a new database. Both work with one plain CloudEvent per line, including its ID and time, so an export imports without any conversion. Since the import computes the hashes itself, you can also export a history, remove personal data from it, and import the result without having to compute any hash by hand.
Incremental backups hold only the events written since a previous backup. A restore takes a full backup followed by its increments, which keeps regular backups of a large database small. Restoring itself has become considerably faster too, since it now writes events in batches.
Faster, and Sturdier Under Load#
Writing is considerably faster, for one client as for many at once, and it no longer slows down as the store grows. Running EventQL queries is considerably faster as well, most of all for queries that read many events, group, sort, or join several sources, and so is reading events. The indexes take far fewer files, so reading the events of a subject gets faster in large databases, and verifying the integrity of the store reports every inconsistency it finds, up to a hundred, rather than only the first.
Much of the other work in 1.3 is invisible until you need it. Every request, every answer, and every idle connection is bounded in time, so a slow or stuck client can no longer hold resources forever. EventQL queries have limits on how deeply they nest and how much memory they hold, which keeps a single query from overflowing the stack or taking as much memory as it likes.
The server compares the API token in constant time and refuses to start with one that could be guessed. And if it fails to store a write, for example because the disk is full, it switches to read-only mode until it is restarted, keeps serving reads, reports this through its health endpoint, and names the cause in its log. Limits lists the bounds.
Running in Production#
A few additions are aimed at running EventSourcingDB in production. Rate limiting is enabled by default and scales with the size of the machine, so a single client that sends far too many requests cannot overwhelm the database. The health endpoint of the v2 API speaks OpenMetrics, which means you can scrape it with Prometheus and similar tools directly, and it reports more about the process, such as its memory and its file descriptors; Logging and Monitoring lists what it reports.
If you want to make sure that only known event types are ever written, the new flag --require-event-schemas rejects writes and restores of events whose type has no registered schema. It is off by default. And an API catalog at /.well-known/api-catalog points tools to the OpenAPI documents of both APIs.
Before You Upgrade#
This release asks for some care when upgrading. Please read Upgrading EventSourcingDB before you start; these are the points that matter most:
- Back up your data first. A data directory that 1.3 has opened cannot be opened by an earlier version again, so a backup is the only way back.
- Stop the old server before you start 1.3. Versions up to 1.2 do not lock the data directory, so a rollout that starts the new server first, such as a Kubernetes Deployment with RollingUpdate, would run two servers on the same data, which can damage it.
- The Docker image runs as another user, UID 65532 instead of 100. A data directory that an earlier image wrote has to be handed over to the new user once, or the container keeps running as the old one; the guide shows both, for Docker and for Kubernetes.
- The API token needs at least 32 characters, unless the server runs with a temporary data directory, and it has to be printable ASCII without whitespace at its start or end. Otherwise, the server refuses to start.
- Update your client SDKs first if your applications verify event hashes, since 1.3 writes a new version of the event hash, and older SDKs report every event written after the upgrade as tampered with.
- The flags --ai-model and --ai-option are gone, since EventAI leaves the management UI; a server that is still started with them no longer starts.
- Check your EventQL queries and preconditions: 1.3 changes, among other things, how values of different types compare, treats the ID of an event as a string, and takes dates and times in UTC, which can change their results or make them fail.
- The first start rebuilds the indexes: 1.3 starts right away and serves reads and writes, but refuses EventQL queries and a few other requests until it is done, which can take several minutes.
The upgrade guide and the changelog list everything else that needs attention, such as stricter rules for the source of events and for event schemas.
Time to Upgrade, or to Start#
Faster where it counts, sturdier where things go wrong, and with a new API next to the one you know: that is 1.3. If you are already running EventSourcingDB, the upgrade guide gets you there safely.
And if you have not tried EventSourcingDB, the database built for Event Sourcing, this is a good moment to start. Installing EventSourcingDB gets you the binaries and the Docker image, and the Quickstart takes you from starting the server to writing and reading a first event in a few minutes. We'd love to hear what you build with it.

articles.title: Val Town is winding down
articles.body:
Dear Val Town community,
We’ve made the difficult decision to wind down Val Town.
You took a big leap of faith to build on us. We thank you for your trust, and we’re sorry we can’t continue to serve you.
The bad news about our business – that we couldn’t compete in the cloud computing space – is good news for you migrating off: there are many wonderful hosting providers you can migrate to, and today’s LLMs are great at these types of migrations. We have guides for migrating to Cloudflare, Vercel, Netlify, and Render. Please reach out if you need help at support@val.town or on Discord.
We are pausing billing today, and will continue servicing existing subscriptions for free. If you pre-paid for our annual plan, we will issue you a partial refund.
Here’s the timeline on our wind-down:
Thank you, the members of the Val Town team, for giving it your all over the past four years. Thank you Tom, Jackson, Charlie, Pete, Potluck, Charmaine, Max, Andre, Sophie, Wolf, Justin, Rodrigo and JP. It was an honor.
Thank you, Dan Levine, for being the best investor I could’ve asked for. Thank you, my other investors, for your trust, support, and capital.
Thank you, our customers and users, for building on us with passion and creativity.
Steve Krouse

One of our favorite multi-filament 3D printers is $100 off

Bambu Lab P2S Combo
